1.pericope_label: From Miletus by Cos, Rhodes and Patara to Tyre, where disciples warned Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem

schools.summary: John Gill says the parting was with great difficulty, with many tears and much wringing of hands, the word signifying that they were plucked from them, since they clung about them as husband and wife and parents and children do, so strong were their affections; and their parting was like the parting of such near relations, or like the plucking of the flesh from the bones, or the drawing and separating of one member from another, such being the cement of true Christian love. The ship they went aboard at Assos went no further, at least in the way the apostle was going, than Patara, Gill says, but lighting on another ship which was bound for Phoenicia, for the city of Tyre, which bordered on the land of Israel and indeed originally belonged to Canaan, they went aboard; and Cyprus, which the Syriac version here calls an island, lay between Syria and Cilicia and was, according to Rabbi Benjamin, four days' sail from Rhodes. At Tyre they found disciples, Gill says, for the Gospel had been preached in Phoenicia by the ministers of the word who were scattered by the persecution raised at the death of Stephen, and here were brethren, such as had believed in Christ, embraced and professed his Gospel, and were baptized in his name, who also had extraordinary gifts as appears by what follows; and there was no doubt a Gospel church founded in this place, though who presided over it in the first century we have no account. In the second century there was a church here and Cassius was bishop of it, Gill continues; in the third century there were martyrs in this place who suffered under Diocletian and bore innumerable stripes with great courage and constancy, and after that fought with beasts, as bears, leopards, boars and bulls, and at the same time Tyrannio, bishop of this church, also suffered martyrdom; in the fourth century there was a synod at Tyre under Constantine, to which he wrote a letter, and a bishop of this church was present at the council of Nice. John Calvin says Luke reckons up briefly the course of his sailing, and that not only to win credit to the history, that we may know what was done in every place, but that the readers may weigh with themselves the invincible and heroic fortitude which was in Paul, who would rather be tossed and troubled with such long, winding and troublesome journeys, that he might serve Christ, than provide for his own quietness. Whereas he says that they were drawn and pulled away, Calvin says, it is not simply referred unto the distance of places, but because the brethren stood on the shore so long as they could see the ship wherein Paul and his companions were carried; and he names the havens where the ship touched for this cause, that we may know that they sailed quietly without trouble of tempest. Let the geographers be consulted touching the situation of the cities whereof he makes mention, Calvin says: it is sufficient for him to show Luke's purpose. Though the number of the faithful was but small, yet there came some seed of the gospel to Tyre, according to the prophecies of the prophets, lest Tyre should be altogether void of the blessing of God, Calvin says; and here, as in other places going before, Luke calls Christians disciples, that we may know that those alone are numbered in the flock of Christ who have embraced his doctrine by faith, for it is a vain and false profession for a man to give his name to Christ and not to understand what he teaches or speaks. Let the readers mark that Paul stayed seven days at Tyre for no other cause save that he might strengthen them, Calvin says, so that we see that whithersoever he came he neglected no occasion to do good. The disciples spoke with the approbation of speech, that Paul might know they spoke by the Spirit of prophecy, Calvin says, and surely this was no small temptation to cause him not to finish the journey he had taken in hand, seeing the Holy Ghost did dissuade him from the same; and this was a very specious pretext to fly from the cross, if he had cared for his own safety, to be drawn back as it were with the hand of God, yet notwithstanding he ceases not to hold on thither whither he knew he was called by the Lord. Here arises a question, Calvin says: how can the brethren dissuade him by the Spirit from doing that which Paul testified he did by the secret motion of the same Spirit, and is the Spirit contrary to himself, that he now looses Paul whom he held bound inwardly? He answers that there are diverse gifts of the Spirit, so that it is no marvel if those who excel in the gift of prophecy be sometimes destitute of judgment or strength: the Lord showed to these brethren what should come to pass, yet nevertheless they know not what is expedient and what Paul's calling requires, because the measure of their gift does not reach so far. And the Lord would have his servant admonished of purpose, Calvin says, partly that through long meditation he might be better furnished and prepared to suffer whatsoever should come, and partly that his constancy might more plainly appear, when, being certified by prophecies of the doleful event, he does notwithstanding wittingly and willingly make haste to endure whatsoever things shall befall him. This was no small testimony of love, Calvin adds, in that they accompanied Paul out of the city with their wives and children, which Luke reports partly that he might commend their godliness according as it deserved and partly that he might declare that Paul had that honour given him which was due to him; whence we also gather that he meant nothing less than to provide for his own commodity, seeing that he was not kept back with so great good will, which was a pleasant bait to entice him to stay. We must also note the solemn custom of praying in weightier affairs, Calvin says, and that being certified by God of the danger they are the more stirred up to pray.

Matthew Henry observes how much ado Paul had to get clear from Ephesus, intimated in the first words of the chapter, that after they had gotten from them, that is, were drawn from them as by violence: it was a force put upon both sides, for Paul was loth to leave them and they were loth to part with him, and yet there was no remedy but so it must be. When good people are taken away by death, Henry says, they are as it were gotten from their friends here below, who struggled hard to have detained them if possible. He then notes what a prosperous voyage they had thence: without any difficulty they came with a straight course, by direct sailing, to Cos, a famous Grecian island, the next day to Rhodes, talked of for the Colossus there, and thence to Patara, a famous port, the metropolis of Lycia; and here they very happily found a ship sailing over into Phoenicia, the very course they were steering. Providence must be acknowledged when things happen thus opportunely, Henry says, and we are favoured by some little circumstances that contribute to the expediting of our affairs, and we must say that it is God that maketh our way perfect. This ship that was bound for Phoenicia, that is Tyre, they took the convenience of, went on board and set sail for Tyre, Henry says; in this voyage they discovered Cyprus, the island that Barnabas was of and which he took care of, and therefore Paul did not visit it, but they left it on the left hand, sailed upon the coast of Syria, and at length landed at Tyre, that celebrated mart of the nations, so it had been but was now reduced, yet something of a trade it had still, for there the ship was to unlade her burden, and did so. When he had arrived there he was upon the coast of the land of Israel, and found now that he could compass the remainder of his journey within the time he had fixed, Henry says; and at Tyre he found disciples, some that had embraced the gospel and professed the Christian faith, for wherever Paul came he enquired what disciples were there, found them out and associated with them, since we know what is the usage with birds of a feather.

Albert Barnes says Cos was a small island in the Grecian Archipelago, a short distance from the south-western point of Asia Minor, now called Stanco, celebrated for its fertility and for the wine and silk-worms which it produced; and Rhodes was an island in the Levant, on which was a city of the same name, principally distinguished for its brazen Colossus, built by Chares of Lyndus, which stood across the mouth of the harbour and was so high that vessels could pass between its legs. It stood fifty-six years and was then thrown down by an earthquake, Barnes says, being reckoned as one of the seven wonders of the world; and when the Saracens took possession of this island they sold this prostrate image to a Jew, who loaded nine hundred camels with the brass of it, this being about the year six hundred, some nine hundred years after it had been thrown down. The ancient name of the island was Asteria, Barnes adds, and its name Rhodes was given from the great quantity of roses which it produced, while Patara was a maritime city of Lycia in Asia Minor over against Rhodes; Tyre was formerly one of the most commercial cities of the world, and it is probable that in the time of Paul its commercial importance had not entirely ceased. This is the first mention of there being Christians at Tyre, Barnes says, but there is no improbability in supposing that the gospel had been preached there though it is not expressly recorded by Luke; their deep interest in Paul's welfare and their apprehension of his danger was the reason why they admonished him not to go. There is some difficulty in understanding the phrase through the Spirit, Barnes says, and in solving it we may remark that it is evident the Holy Spirit is meant and that Luke means to say this was spoken by his inspiration, the Holy Spirit having been bestowed on Christians at that time in large measures; that it was not understood by Paul as a positive command that he should not go up to Jerusalem, for had it been, it would not have been disobeyed, Paul evidently understanding it as expressive of their earnest wish that he should not go, as apprizing him of danger; and that it is to be understood therefore simply as an inspired prophetic warning that if he went, he went at the risk of his life, joined with their individual personal wishes. Paul was in better circumstances to understand this than we are, Barnes says, and his interpretation was doubtless correct; Grotius renders it that he should not go unless he was willing to be bound, Michaelis and Stolzius that they gave him prophetic warning that he should not go to Jerusalem, and Doddridge that if he tendered his own liberty and safety he should not go up, since it would certainly expose him to very great hazard. The inspiration in the case was that of admonition and warning, not of positive command, Barnes concludes: Paul was simply apprized of the danger and then left to the free determination of his own will, and he chose to encounter the danger of which he was thus apprized, not despising the intimations of the Spirit but judging that his duty to God called him thus to encounter the hazards of the journey; we may be apprized of danger in a certain course, either by our friends or by the word of God, and still it may be our duty to meet it, since our duty is not to be measured by the fact that we shall experience dangers, in whatever way that may be made known to us. On the parting at the shore Barnes says that any place may be proper for prayer, God being everywhere and able as easily to hear the prayer of the humble on the sea-shore as in the most magnificent temple; and this is an instance where the apostle evidently prayed with the church without a form of prayer, for no man can believe that he thus poured forth the desires of his heart at parting, and commended them to God, in a prescribed form of words. Besides that, there is not the least evidence that such a form was then used in the Christian church, Barnes says: scenes like this show more clearly than abstract arguments could do that such a form was not needed and would not be used, since Paul and his fellow Christians on the sand of the sea-shore would pour forth the gushing emotions of their souls in language such as their circumstances would suggest, and it is presumed to be impossible that any man can read this narrative in a dispassionate manner without believing that they offered an extempore prayer. Charles Ellicott says the Greek verb is more emphatic than the English and might almost be rendered, when we had torn ourselves away from them, and that the navigation is, as before, from port to port; it would hardly be within the scope of a commentary to enter at length into the history of each place, but it will be enough to note that Cos was famous both for its wines and its silk fabrics, of fine and almost transparent tissue, that Rhodes, then famous for its Colossus, was one of the largest and most flourishing islands of the Archipelago and is memorable for us in later history as connected with the Knights Hospitallers of St John, and that Patara was a harbour on the coast of Lycia. For this harbour the ship in which the travellers had left Troas and Miletus was bound, Ellicott says, and they had therefore to look out for another; happily there was no long delay, and they embarked at once on a merchant-ship bound for Phoenicia. The use of a technical term about sighting Cyprus is specially characteristic of Luke, Ellicott says, the meaning being that as soon as they sighted the island they stood to the south-east and so had it on their left as they continued their voyage to Syria. The word for finding disciples implies a previous search, Ellicott says: they inquired, when they landed amid the crowded streets of the still busy port, whether any Christians were to be found there, and it will be remembered that Paul had passed through that region at least once before, the church having probably been planted by the labours of Philip as the Evangelist of Caesarea. The seven days' stay, as at Troas and afterwards at Puteoli, was obviously for the purpose of attending one, or possibly more than one, meeting of the church for the Lord's Supper on the Lord's Day, Ellicott says, and the utterances through the Spirit implied the exercise of prophetic gifts at such a meeting. It seems at first somewhat startling that Paul should reject what is described as an inspired counsel, Ellicott says, or, if we believe him also to have been guided by the Spirit, that the two inspirations should thus clash; we remember, however, that men received the Spirit by measure, and the prophets of the churches at Tyre, as elsewhere, though foreseeing the danger to which the Apostle was exposed, might yet be lacking in that higher inspiration which guided the decision of the Apostle, and which he himself defines as the spirit of power and of love and of a sound mind. This is, it is believed, a much more adequate explanation than that which sees in the Apostle's conduct a somewhat self-willed adherence to his own human purpose, and finds a chastisement for that self-will in the long delay and imprisonment that followed on the slighted warnings, Ellicott says: he was right, we may boldly say, to go to Jerusalem in spite of consequences, and the repeated warnings are an indication of the exceeding bitterness of feeling with which the Judaisers and unbelieving Jews were known to be animated against him. The tense of the departure brings before us something like a procession wending its way from the city to the shore, Ellicott says, and the choice of the place was natural enough, being the spot where the two sets of friends were to part and removed from the stir and bustle of the city; we may add that it fell in with the common Jewish practice of using the banks of rivers or the seashore as a place of prayer, so that the beach of Tyre became for the time a place of prayer, and it seems implied from the use of the plural that Paul was not the only spokesman of the prayers but that others also joined in reciprocal intercession. The article before the ship probably, though not necessarily, indicates that they went in the same ship that had brought them, Ellicott adds, and which, after discharging her cargo at Tyre, was now bound for Caesarea. A.T. Robertson says the participle for parting is the same verb used elsewhere of drawing away and of the Lord withdrawing in the garden, and that the phrase for a straight course is the one Luke used of the voyage from Troas to Samothrace. Cos stands today about forty nautical miles south from Miletus, an island famous as the birthplace of Hippocrates and Apelles with a great medical school, and a great trading place with many Jews, Robertson says; Rhodes is called the island of roses, since the sun shone most days and made roses luxuriant, and the great colossus which represented the sun, one of the seven wonders of the world, was prostrate at this time, the island lying at the entrance to the Aegean and having a great university, especially for rhetoric and oratory. Patara was a seaport on the Lycian coast on the left bank of the Xanthus, Robertson says, which once had an oracle of Apollo that rivalled that at Delphi, and this was the course taken by hundreds of ships every season. Paul had used a small coasting vessel, probably hired, that anchored each night at Cos, Rhodes and Patara, Robertson says, and he was still some four hundred miles from Jerusalem, but at Patara he caught a large merchantman that could sail across the open sea. The participle for coming in sight of Cyprus is a Doric form of an old verb meaning to make appear or bring to light, that is, having made Cyprus rise up out of the sea, Robertson says, these being nautical terms found in the New Testament only here and in Luke; they sailed south of Cyprus and kept on sailing till they came to Syria, coming down to Tyre, then a free city of Syria in honour of its former greatness. The periphrastic imperfect means that thither the boat was unloading her cargo, Robertson says, the word for burden meaning a cargo and occurring only here and in the Revelation, the ship being probably a grain or fruit ship, and it took seven days here to unload and reload. The participle for having found means to find by searching, Robertson says: there was a church here, but it was a large city and the number of members may not have been large, probably some of those who fled from Jerusalem and came to Phoenicia having started the work. Through the Spirit means undoubtedly the Holy Spirit, who had already told Paul that bonds and afflictions awaited him in Jerusalem, Robertson says, and the indirect command is not to keep on going to Jerusalem; in spite of this warning Paul felt it his duty as before to go on, evidently interpreting the action of the Holy Spirit as information and warning although the disciples at Tyre gave it the form of a prohibition, since duty called louder than warning to Paul even if both were the calls of God. There is no word for and in the Greek of the farewell, Robertson says, simply a genitive absolute, they all with wives and children accompanying us, just as at Miletus, and this is the first mention of children in connection with the apostolic churches, as Vincent notes, a vivid picture here as at Miletus and an evident touch of an eyewitness. This scene is in public as at Miletus, but they did not care, Robertson says, and the verb for bidding farewell is a rare compound found here alone in the New Testament, a tender scene, but with, as Furneaux says, no bonds of long comradeship, none of the clinging love seen at Miletus; and the phrase for home again means to their own places, the idiom used of the Beloved Disciple and of Jesus in the Gospel of John.

Adam Clarke summarises the chapter before expounding it, that Paul and his company sail from Miletus and come to Cos, Rhodes and Patara, find a Phoenician ship at Patara, go on board, sail past Cyprus and land at Tyre, where they find disciples and stay seven days and are kindly entertained; that after bidding the disciples farewell they take ship and sail to Ptolemais, salute the brethren, stay one day, come to Caesarea and lodge with Philip, one of the seven deacons; that there Agabus the prophet foretells Paul's persecution at Jerusalem and the disciples endeavour to dissuade him, but he is resolute; that they are kindly received by James and the elders, who advise Paul, because of the Jews, to show his respect for the law of Moses by purifying himself with certain others under a vow; and that some of the Asiatic Jews, finding him in the temple, raise an insurrection against him, from which the chief captain rescues him. Coming with a straight course implies, Clarke says, that they had wind and tide in their favour. Cos was an island in the Archipelago, one of those called the Sporades, famous for the worship of Aesculapius and Juno and for being the birthplace of Hippocrates, the most eminent of physicians, and Apelles, the most celebrated of painters, Clarke says; Rhodes was another island in the same sea, celebrated for its Colossus, which was one of the seven wonders of the world, a brazen statue of Apollo so high that ships in full sail could pass between its legs, the work of Chares, a pupil of Lysippus, who spent twelve years in making it. It was a hundred and six feet high and so great that few people could fathom its thumb, Clarke says, and it was thrown down by an earthquake about two hundred and twenty-four years before Christ, after having stood sixty-six years; when the Saracens took possession of this island they sold this prostrate image to a Jew, who loaded nine hundred camels with the brass of it, this being about the year six hundred and sixty, nearly nine hundred years after it had been thrown down. We cannot understand the warning as a command from the Holy Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem, Clarke says, else Paul must have been highly criminal to have disobeyed it: through the Spirit must either refer to the disciples' own great earnestness to dissuade him from a journey which they plainly saw would be injurious to him, and so Bishop Pearce understands this place, or, if it refer to the Holy Spirit, it must mean that if he regarded his personal safety he must not at this time go up to Jerusalem. The Spirit foretold Paul's persecutions but does not appear to have forbidden his journey, Clarke says, and Paul was persuaded that in acting as he was about to do, whatever personal risk he ran, he should bring more glory to God by going to Jerusalem than by tarrying at Tyre or elsewhere; the purport of this divine communication was that if he went up the Jews would persecute him and he would be imprisoned, and as he was apprized of this he might have desisted, for the whole was conditional. The Holy Spirit neither commanded him to go nor forbade him, Clarke says, the whole being conditional and he being left to the free exercise of his own judgment and conscience; this was a similar case to that of David in Keilah, for David prevented the threatened evil by leaving Keilah, while Paul fell into it by going to Jerusalem. It is not likely that Paul, Silas and Luke had either wives or children with them, Clarke says, and it is more natural to suppose that the brethren of Tyre with their wives and children are those meant, who through affection to the apostles accompanied them from their homes to the ship, the coming out of the husbands, wives and children showing what a general and affectionate interest the preaching and private conversation of these holy men had excited. As God fills heaven and earth, so he may be worshipped everywhere, Clarke says, as well on the seashore, when circumstances require it, as in the temple; we have already seen in the case of Lydia that the Jews had places of prayer by the river sides, and an observation in Tertullian seems to intimate that they preferred such places and in the open air offered their petitions to God by the seashore. The taking of leave means having given each other the kiss of peace, as was the constant custom of the Jews and primitive Christians, Clarke adds, and those who returned home were the men, their wives and their children. John Wesley says they were torn away from them, not without doing violence both to themselves and them; that it was foretold in the psalm that there should be Christians at Tyre; and that they tarried there seven days in order to spend a Sabbath with them. Who told Paul by the Spirit means that afflictions awaited him at Jerusalem, Wesley says, and this was properly what they said by the Spirit, while they themselves advised him not to go up: the disciples seemed to understand their prophetic impulse to be an intimation from the Spirit that Paul, if he were so minded, might avoid the danger by not going to Jerusalem.

debates: Whether the Spirit forbade the journey: Barnes denies it was a positive command, since had it been, Paul would not have disobeyed it, and reports Grotius, Michaelis, Stolzius and Doddridge to like effect; Clarke says a command would have made Paul highly criminal, and offers Bishop Pearce's reading that the phrase refers to the disciples' own earnestness; Calvin and Ellicott independently answer from the diversity of gifts, that men receive the Spirit by measure and prophets may foresee an event without knowing what is expedient; Robertson holds that Paul took as information what the disciples gave the form of a prohibition; Wesley says they understood their impulse as an intimation that he might avoid the danger if he were so minded

Whether Paul was right to go: Ellicott rejects the reading that finds a self-willed adherence to his own purpose and a chastisement for it in the imprisonment that followed, and says boldly that he was right to go in spite of consequences; Calvin holds the warnings were sent on purpose, that by long meditation he might be prepared and his constancy appear; Clarke compares David at Keilah, who prevented the threatened evil by leaving, where Paul fell into it by going

What the prayer on the beach shows: Barnes makes it an argument that no prescribed form of prayer was used or needed in the apostolic church, and that no one can read the narrative dispassionately and think otherwise; Ellicott and Clarke read the same scene as Jewish custom continued, the shore being a recognised place of prayer, Clarke citing Tertullian

How much geography a commentator owes: Calvin refers the reader to the geographers and says it is enough for him to show Luke's purpose; Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all supply the histories of Cos, Rhodes, Patara and Tyre at length
outliers: The two accounts of the Colossus differ twice on figures, Barnes giving fifty-six years standing and a sale about the year six hundred, Clarke sixty-six years and about six hundred and sixty, though the nine hundred camel-loads of brass are common to both
Robertson's observation that the great statue was already lying prostrate when Paul's ship passed Rhodes

Gill's excursus on the later church at Tyre, with Cassius its second-century bishop, martyrs under Diocletian who fought with bears, leopards, boars and bulls, and the synod held there under Constantine
Clarke's report from Tertullian that the Jews preferred the open shore and sent up their petitions to heaven along it
Furneaux's remark, quoted by Robertson, that the farewell at Tyre had no bonds of long comradeship and none of the clinging love shown at Miletus
Henry's turn of the opening verb into a figure of death, that good people are gotten from friends below who would have detained them if they could

7.pericope_label: From Ptolemais to Caesarea, lodging with Philip the evangelist, one of the seven, whose four unmarried daughters prophesied

schools.summary: John Gill says they finished their course from Tyre, that is sailed from thence, and that the next day those of Paul's company departed from Ptolemais, namely Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Timothy, Tychicus, Trophimus and Luke, the writer of this history. The same man had four daughters, Gill observes, so that he was a married man, which may be observed against the Papists, who forbid marriage to ecclesiastics. John Calvin says Luke briefly declares that Paul was also received at Ptolemais by the brethren, a city of Phoenicia standing upon the sea-coast not far from the borders of Judea, from which Paul and his companions had no long journey to Caesarea; but if the readers are disposed to know further touching the situation of regions, let them resort to the geographers. He says that when Paul came to Caesarea they lodged with Philip, whom he calls an Evangelist though he was one of the seven deacons, Calvin continues, and by this we may easily gather that that deaconship was an office which continued but for a time, because it had not otherwise been lawful for Philip to forsake Jerusalem and to go to Caesarea; and in this place he is set before us not as a voluntary forsaker of his office but as one to whom a greater and more excellent charge was committed. The evangelists, in Calvin's judgment, were in the midst between apostles and doctors, for it was a function next to the apostles to preach the gospel in all places and not to have any certain place of abode, only the degree of honour was inferior; for when Paul describes the order of the Church he so puts them after the apostles that he shows they have more room given them where they may teach than the pastors, who are tied to certain places. Therefore Philip did for a time exercise the office of a deacon at Jerusalem, Calvin concludes, whom the Church thought afterward to be a meet man to whom the treasure of the gospel should be committed. On the daughters Calvin says this is added for the commendation of Philip, not only that we might know that his house was well ordered but also that it was famous and excellent through the blessing of God, for assuredly it was no small gift to have four daughters all endowed with the spirit of prophecy. By this means the Lord meant to beautify the first beginnings of the gospel, Calvin says, when he raised up men and women to foretell things to come: prophecies had now almost ceased many years among the Jews, to the end they might be more attentive and desirous to hear the new voice of the gospel, and therefore, seeing that prophesying, which was in a manner quite ceased, does now after long time return again, it was a token of a more perfect state. Notwithstanding, it seems that the same was the reason why it ceased shortly after, Calvin says, for God did support the old people with diverse foretellings until Christ should make an end of all prophecies by his coming; therefore it was meet that the new kingdom of Christ should be thus furnished and beautified with this furniture, that all men might know that that promised visitation of the Lord was present, and it was also expedient that it should last but for a short time, lest the faithful should always wait for some further thing, or lest curious wits might have occasion given to seek or invent some new thing ever now and then. For we know that when that ability and skill was taken away there were notwithstanding many brain-sick fellows who did boast that they were prophets, Calvin says, and also it may be that the frowardness of men did deprive the Church of this gift; but that one cause ought to be sufficient, in that God, by taking away prophecies, did testify that the end and perfection was present in Christ. It is uncertain how these maids did execute the office of prophesying, Calvin adds, saving that the Spirit of God did so guide and govern them that he did not overthrow the order which he himself set down; and forasmuch as he does not suffer women to bear any public office in the Church, it is to be thought that they did prophesy at home, or in some private place, without the common assembly.

Matthew Henry says we have here Paul and his company arrived at length at Caesarea, where he designed to make some stay, it being the place where the gospel was first preached to the Gentiles and the Holy Ghost fell upon them. He seldom had occasion to go to a public house, Henry observes, but wherever he came some friend or other took him in and bade him welcome; and those that had sailed together parted when the voyage was accomplished, according as their business was, for those concerned in the cargo stayed where the ship was to unlade her burden and others, when they came to Ptolemais, went as their occasions led them, but those of Paul's company went where he went and came to Caesarea. Those that travel together through this world will separate at death, Henry says, and then it will appear who are of Paul's company and who are not. At Caesarea they were entertained by Philip the evangelist, whom we left there many years ago after he had baptized the eunuch, and there we now find him again, Henry says: he was originally a deacon, one of the seven chosen to serve tables; he was now and had long been an evangelist, one that went about to plant and water churches as the apostles did and gave himself, as they did, to the word and prayer, so that having used the office of a deacon well he purchased to himself a good degree, and having been faithful in a few things was made ruler over many things; and he had a house at Caesarea fit to entertain Paul and all his company, and bade them very welcome to it. Thus does it become Christians and ministers, according as their ability is, to use hospitality one to another without grudging, Henry says. This Philip had four maiden daughters who did prophesy, Henry continues, which intimates that they prophesied of Paul's troubles at Jerusalem, as others had done, and dissuaded him from going, or perhaps they prophesied for his comfort and encouragement in reference to the difficulties that were before him; and here was a further accomplishment of the prophecy of Joel, of such a plentiful pouring out of the Spirit upon all flesh that their sons and their daughters should prophesy, that is, foretell things to come.

Albert Barnes says Ptolemais was a city situated on the coast of the Mediterranean, on the north angle of a bay which extends in a semicircle of three leagues as far as the point of Mount Carmel, washed by the sea at the south and west sides and surrounded by triple walls. It was in the tribe of Asher and was originally called Accho, Barnes says, but was called Ptolemais in honour of one of the Ptolemies who beautified and adorned it; the Christian crusaders gave it the name of Acre, or St John of Acre, from a magnificent church built in it and dedicated to the apostle John, and it is still called Akka by the Turks, while the Syriac and Arabic render it Accho in this place. It sustained several sieges during the crusades, Barnes continues, and was the last fortified place wrested from the Christians by the Turks; it sustained a memorable siege by Bonaparte, and since then has been much increased and strengthened, and it surrendered to the British fleet under Admiral Stopford on the third of November, eighteen hundred and forty, after a few hours' resistance, its present population being estimated at from eighteen to twenty thousand. On the clause about Paul's company Barnes says that from this it would appear they had been attended thus far by some persons who were going only to Ptolemais, but that this clause is wanting in many manuscripts and has been omitted by Bengel, Griesbach, Knapp and others as spurious, being also wanting in the Syriac and the Vulgate. The word evangelist properly means one who announces good news, Barnes says, and in the New Testament is applied to a preacher of the gospel or one who declares the glad tidings of salvation, occurring only in two other places; what was the precise rank of those who bore this title in the early Christian church cannot perhaps be determined, but it is evident that it is used to denote the office of preaching the gospel, and as this title is applied to Philip and not to any other of the seven deacons it would seem probable that he had been entrusted with a special commission to preach, and that preaching did not pertain to him as a deacon and does not properly belong to that office, the business of a deacon being to take care of the poor members of the church. The office of preaching was distinct from this, Barnes says, though, as in this case, it might be conferred on the same individual. That females sometimes partook of the prophetic influence and foretold future events is evident from various places in the New Testament, he adds. Charles Ellicott says Ptolemais is memorable both for its antiquity and for the varied fortunes of its city: as Accho it appears in the book of Judges as one of the old cities of the Canaanites which the Israelites of the tribe of Asher failed to conquer, and it was conquered, rebuilt and renamed by Ptolemy Soter king of Egypt, though the old name ultimately revived, or perhaps was never entirely disused, so that the natives of the region still speak of it as Accho while to Europeans it is familiar as Acre, or more fully St Jean d'Acre. Here also, as through all the line of cities along the coast, we find a church already organised, Ellicott says, founded probably by Philip the Evangelist; and here the stay of the travellers was shorter than at Tyre, probably because the ship only put into the harbour for the night, though the passengers had time to land and refresh themselves by intercourse with those who were sharers in their faith and hope. The Greek which answers to the intervening five words about Paul's company is wanting in the best manuscripts and seems a needless interpolation, Ellicott says, there being no apparent reason for any change in the writer's previous phraseology or for his distinguishing Paul's company from some other person or persons unknown; and in some of the manuscripts in which it is found the verb is in the third person. This was Paul's third visit to Caesarea, Ellicott notes, and we may well believe that he was simply renewing the intercourse of a previous friendship with Philip. The title given to Philip is interesting as showing that the work of serving tables, that is of superintending the distribution of alms, had been merged in the higher work of a missionary preacher, Ellicott says: he was no longer known, if indeed that title had ever been applied to him, as Philip the deacon, but as Philip the evangelist. The office so described is recognised by Paul in his enumeration of spiritual gifts and functions as coming next in order of importance to those of apostles and prophets and before pastors and teachers, Ellicott continues, and it would seem accordingly to have been distinct from the orders, in the later sense, of presbyter or deacon, though capable of being united with either of them; Timothy was exhorted by Paul, when left at Ephesus with the authority of a vicar apostolic, to do the work of an evangelist as that to which he had been called. It followed from the nature of the office, as analogous to that of the missionary of later times, that though residing mainly at Caesarea Philip's labours extended beyond its limits, Ellicott says, and we have seen reason to trace his work all along the coasts of Palestine and Phoenicia. As far as we know Philip and Luke had not met before, Ellicott adds, and we can imagine the satisfaction with which the latter, himself probably an evangelist in both senses of the word and already contemplating his work as an historian, would welcome the acquaintance of the former, how he would ask many questions as to the early history of the Church and learn from him all, or nearly all, that we find in the first eleven chapters of this book. We note how entirely the Seven are regarded as a special or distinct body, Ellicott says: if the term deacon had ever been applied to them, which is very doubtful, it ceased to be applicable by its wide extension to the subordinate functionaries of the churches throughout the empire. On the daughters Ellicott says both elements of the description are full of interest as throwing light on the life of the Apostolic Church. The word virgins then, as afterwards, probably indicated not merely the bare fact that they were as yet unmarried but that they had devoted themselves, if not by irrevocable vows yet by a steadfast purpose, to that form of service, Ellicott says: in the organisation of women's work in the Church they formed apparently a distinct class, the complement of that of the widows, and Paul had distinctly sanctioned such a life as presenting a higher standard of excellence than the duties of domestic life, on grounds which in their general character went beyond the present distress of a time of persecution. It was, indeed, a matter on which he had no commandment from the Lord, Ellicott says, and in which he was therefore open to the teachings of experience, and these seem to have modified his judgment at a later date and led him to the conclusion that it was better that the younger widows should marry, and that they should only be received into the list of those maintained by the Church at a more advanced age. The order of virgin, however, continued to exist, Ellicott says, and the term is found, sometimes with the handmaid of the Lord added to it, in the inscriptions from the catacombs now in the Museums of the Collegio Romano and the Lateran, while Pliny in his letter to Trajan speaks of the women who were then called ministrae among the Christians, the latter term being probably used as the equivalent for deaconesses. The word prophesy comprised much more than mere prediction of the future and included all words that came into the mind of the speaker as an inspiration, and to the hearers as a message from God, Ellicott says: in other words, they preached, and we ask when and where, and whether they prophesied in the assemblies of the Church. It is true that Paul had forbidden this at Corinth and forbade it afterwards at Ephesus, Ellicott says, but the very prohibition proves that the practice was common, and it does not follow that Paul's rules of discipline as yet obtained in all the churches; it is perfectly possible, however, that they may have confined their ministrations to those of their own sex and, accompanying their father in his missionary journeys, have gained access to women both among Jews and Gentiles and brought them to the knowledge of the Truth, since it is obvious that the services of women acting as deaconesses would be needed as a matter of decorum in the baptism of female converts. A.T. Robertson says the participle for finishing is of an old verb meaning to accomplish thoroughly, found only here in the New Testament, and that Page and Hackett take the phrase from Tyre with the verb of arriving rather than with the voyage, and with good reason: having thereby finished the voyage, we arrived from Tyre at Ptolemais. Ptolemais is the modern Acre, called Accho in the book of Judges, Robertson says, its harbour the best on the coast of Palestine and surrounded by mountains, about thirty miles south of Tyre; it was never taken by Israel and was considered a Philistine town, while the Greeks counted it a Phoenician city, and it was the key to the road down the coast between Syria and Egypt, having successively the rule of the Ptolemies, Syrians and Romans. The word here is greeting rather than farewell, Robertson notes, and the stay was short, one day, but the brethren Paul and his party found easily, the scattered brethren possibly having founded the church here, or Philip may have done it. Caesarea is the political capital of Judea under the Romans, where the procurators lived, Robertson says, a city of importance built by Herod the Great and named in honour of Augustus, with a magnificent harbour and mostly Greek inhabitants; this is the third time we have seen Paul there, and the best manuscripts omit the phrase about Paul's company. Philip is second in the list of the seven after Stephen, and that fact is mentioned here, Robertson says, this title distinguishing him from Philip the apostle, one of the twelve; his evangelistic work followed the death of Stephen, in Samaria and Philistia, with his home in Caesarea. This is the earliest of the three New Testament examples of the word evangelist, Robertson says, apparently a word used to describe one who told the gospel story as Philip did, and may have been used of him first of all as John was termed the baptizer and then the Baptist; it is found on an inscription in one of the Greek islands of uncertain date and was used by ecclesiastical writers of later times of the Four Gospels as we do. As used here the meaning is a travelling missionary who gospelized communities, Robertson says, and in the letter to the Ephesians the word seems to describe a special class of ministers just as we have them today, men having different gifts, while the ideal minister today combines the gifts of evangelist, herald, teacher and shepherd. The phrase for abiding with him is a neat idiom for at his house, Robertson says, and what a joyful time Paul had in conversation with Philip, since he could learn from him much of value about the early days of the gospel in Jerusalem; and Luke could, and probably did, take notes from Philip and his daughters about the beginnings of Christian history, for it is generally supposed that the we sections of Acts represent a travel document by Luke, so that we may suppose he is already gathering data for future use, and if so, these were precious days for him. On the daughters Robertson says this is not necessarily an order of virgins, but Philip had the honour of having in his home four virgin daughters with the gift of prophecy, which was not necessarily predicting events though that was done as by Agabus here: it was more than ordinary preaching and was put by Paul above the other gifts like tongues. The prophecy of Joel about their sons and daughters prophesying is quoted by Peter and applied to the events on the day of Pentecost, Robertson says, and Paul gives directions about praying and prophesying by the women, apparently in public worship, with the head covered, though not forbidding the praying and prophesying; with this must be compared his demand for silence by the women elsewhere, which it is not easy to reconcile, and one wonders if there was not something known to Paul about special conditions in Corinth and Ephesus that he has not told. There was also Anna the prophetess in the temple, Robertson adds, besides the inspired hymns of Elizabeth and of Mary, and there were Old Testament prophetesses like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah, but at any rate there was no order of women prophets or official ministers; today in our Sunday schools the women do most of the actual teaching, and the whole problem is difficult and calls for restraint and reverence, though one thing is certain, that Luke appreciated the services of women for Christ, as is shown often in his writings before this incident.

Adam Clarke says Ptolemais was a seaport town of Galilee, not far from Mount Carmel, between Tyre and Caesarea, where the river Belus empties itself into the sea; it was at first called Accho, and this is the reading of the Syriac and Arabic, and belonged to the tribe of Asher, and it was enlarged and beautified by the first of the Egyptian Ptolemies, from whom it was called Ptolemais. This place terminated Paul's voyage, Clarke says, and this is what is expressed in the text, that they came from Tyre to Ptolemais, where their voyage ended. The clause about Paul's company is wanting in four of the uncials and many others, Clarke notes, and in the Syriac, Coptic, Vulgate and Armenian. Caesarea was Caesarea of Palestine, already sufficiently described, and Philip the evangelist was one of the seven deacons, who seems to have settled here after he had baptized the eunuch, Clarke says. On the four daughters who did prophesy Clarke says these were probably no more than teachers in the Church, for we have already seen that this is a frequent meaning of the word prophesy, and this is undoubtedly one thing intended by the prophecy of Joel quoted earlier in this book; and if Philip's daughters might be prophetesses, why not teachers. John Wesley says that having finished their voyage from Macedonia they came to Ptolemais, a celebrated city on the sea coast anciently called Accho, which is now, like many other once noble cities, only a heap of ruins. Caesarea was so called from a stately temple which Herod the Great dedicated there to Augustus Caesar, Wesley says, and was the place where the Roman governor of Judea generally resided and kept his court. An evangelist is a preacher of the Gospel to those who had never heard it, as Philip had done to the Samaritans, to the Ethiopian eunuch and to all the towns from Azotus to Caesarea, Wesley says, and it is not unlikely he spent the following years preaching in Tyre and Sidon and the other heathen cities in the neighbourhood of Galilee, his house being at Caesarea, a convenient situation for that purpose; and they lodged at his house during their stay.

debates: Whether the clause about Paul's company belongs to the text: Ellicott calls it a needless interpolation wanting in the best manuscripts, and notes that where it is found some copies read the verb in the third person; Barnes reports it omitted as spurious by Bengel, Griesbach and Knapp and absent from the Syriac and Vulgate; Clarke lists four uncials and four versions against it; Robertson says the best manuscripts omit it; yet Gill expounds it as genuine and names the seven who made up the company, and Henry draws from it the reflection that those who travel together through this world will separate at death

How the four daughters exercised their gift: Ellicott takes them for a recognised class answering to the widows, holds that the very prohibition of women speaking proves the practice was common, and says Paul was open to the teachings of experience and modified his judgment later; Robertson finds the prohibitions hard to reconcile with the permission elsewhere and wonders whether Paul knew local conditions he has not told; Calvin, holding that women bear no public office, concludes they prophesied at home or in private; Clarke supposes they were no more than teachers; Henry takes them to have prophesied about Paul's own troubles

What Philip's title implies about the diaconate: Barnes argues that since the word is used of him and of none of the other six, preaching was a special commission and no part of a deacon's office; Calvin infers that the deaconship itself continued only for a time, else Philip could not lawfully have left Jerusalem, and ranks evangelists between apostles and doctors; Ellicott holds the office distinct from the later orders though capable of union with either, and doubts the term deacon was ever applied to the Seven at all
What state the old city was in: Barnes describes a living town of some twenty thousand, lately surrendered to a British fleet after a few hours' resistance; Wesley says it is now only a heap of ruins
outliers: The joint conjecture of Ellicott and Robertson that Luke gathered here, from Philip and his daughters, all or nearly all of what stands in the first eleven chapters of this book
Ellicott's appeal to the catacomb inscriptions in the Collegio Romano and the Lateran, and to Pliny's letter to Trajan on the women called ministrae
Robertson's remark that today in our Sunday schools the women do most of the actual teaching, and that the whole problem calls for restraint and reverence
Calvin's account of why prophecy was restored and then withdrawn, that God by taking it away testified that the end and perfection was present in Christ
Gill's inference from Philip's four daughters that he was a married man, observed against those who forbid marriage to the clergy
Robertson's suggestion that the word evangelist may have been coined of Philip as the title of Baptist was coined of John

10.pericope_label: Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s girdle, the company entreats him with tears, and he answers that he is ready to die

schools.summary: John Gill says it is not stated how many days they tarried, but it could not be very many if the apostle got to Jerusalem by Pentecost as he desired; that Agabus came to them in Philip's house; that when they heard these prophecies concerning the binding of the apostle by the Jews and the delivery of him to the Romans, they also saw the symbolical representations of these things; that they were crying about him, both his companions and the disciples of Caesarea, which affected him and gave him great uneasiness, even more than the prophecies of Agabus did; and that he would not be persuaded, but was determined to go to Jerusalem at all events. John Calvin says that though Luke does not plainly express the same, yet he conjectures that this Agabus was the same of whom mention is made in the eleventh chapter, who foretold that there should be famine under the reign of Claudius Caesar; and when Luke calls him a prophet, as of late he called the four daughters of Philip, he signifies that it was not a common but a peculiar gift. Now we must see to what end the persecution which was at hand was now again shown by Agabus, Calvin says: as concerning Paul, he had been more than sufficiently warned already, and therefore he does not doubt but that this confirmation was added for other men's sake, because the Lord meant everywhere to make known the bonds of his servant, partly that they might know that he entered the combat willingly, partly that they might perceive that he was appointed of God to be a champion to fight for the gospel. It was surely a profitable example of invincible constancy, Calvin says, seeing that he offered himself willingly and wittingly to the violence of the adversaries; and no less profitable is it for us at this day that his apostleship should be confirmed with this voluntary and no less constant giving over of his life. It was a usual thing among the prophets to represent those things which they spoke by signs, Calvin continues, neither did they confirm their prophecies by using signs through their own motion but at the commandment of the Spirit, as when Isaiah is commanded to go barefoot, Jeremiah to put a yoke upon his neck and to sell the possession and buy it, and Ezekiel to dig through the wall of his house privily and in the same night to carry forth burdens. These and such like might seem to the common sort to be toys, Calvin says, but the same Spirit who did apply signs to his words did inwardly touch the hearts of the godly, as if they had been brought to the very thing itself; so this spectacle mentioned by Luke did no less move Paul's companions than if they had seen him bound indeed. The false prophets did afterward essay to delude the simple by this policy, Calvin adds, as Satan is in a manner God's ape and his ministers do envy the servants of God: Zedekiah made himself horns wherewith he promised Syria should be pushed, and Ananias, by breaking Jeremiah's yoke, put the people in a vain hope of deliverance. Because they had not all one revelation, it is no marvel if their judgments were diverse, Calvin says: seeing these holy men knew that there consisted much in the life or death of one man, they would not have him come into danger rashly, and their desire is worthy of praise, in that they desired to provide for the common safety of the Church by keeping back Paul. But on the other side Paul's constancy deserves so much the more praise, Calvin continues, when he continues so steadfast in the calling of God, for he was not ignorant what great trouble he should suffer by reason of his bands; but because he knows the will of God, which was his only rule in taking counsel, he makes no account of all other things that he may follow it. Assuredly we must be so subject to the will and pleasure of God that no profit, no kind of reason may remove us from obeying him, Calvin says. When Paul reprehends the brethren because they afflict his heart with weeping, he sufficiently declares that he was not hardened but that he was brought unto some feeling and suffering together with them, Calvin says: therefore the tears of the godly did wound his heart, but that softness did not turn him out of the way, but that he proceeded to follow God with a straight course; therefore we must use such courtesy toward our brethren that the will of God have always the upper hand. Paul does again declare by his answer, Calvin adds, that the servants of Christ cannot be prepared to do their duty unless they despise death, and that none can ever be well encouraged to live to the Lord but those who will willingly lay down their lives for the testimony of the truth. If they had thought that he ran rashly unto death they would not have ceased so, Calvin says: therefore they yield lest they resist the Holy Spirit, whereby they understand that Paul is governed; for that which they had heard before by the mouth of Paul, that he was drawn as it were by the bands of the Spirit, was quite out of their heads by reason of the sorrow which they had conceived, but when they are taught again that it was the will of God that it should be so, they think it unlawful for them to resist any longer. With this bridle must all our affections be kept in, Calvin concludes, that nothing be so bitter, or doleful, or hard, which the will of God may not mitigate and mollify; for so often as anything hard or sharp falls out, we give God small honour unless this thought prevail with us, that we must obey him.

Albert Barnes says the loose, flowing robes or outer garments worn in eastern countries were bound by a girdle or sash around the body when men ran or laboured or walked, so that such a girdle was an indispensable part of dress; and Agabus bound his own hands and feet as emblematic of what would be done by the Jews to Paul. It was common for the prophets to perform actions which were emblematic of the events they predicted, Barnes says, the design being to make the prediction more forcible and impressive by representing it to the eye: thus Jeremiah was directed to bury his girdle by the Euphrates to denote the approaching captivity of the Jews, and to make bands and yokes and put them round his neck as a sign to Edom and Moab; thus the act of the potter was emblematic of the destruction coming upon the nation; and so Isaiah walked naked and barefoot as a sign of the captivity of Egypt and Ethiopia. This was fulfilled, Barnes says, and the delivery into the hands of the Gentiles means to be tried, for the Romans then had jurisdiction over Judea. What mean ye is a tender and affectionate but firm reproach, Barnes says: to weep and break his heart is to afflict him and distract his mind by alarms and by the expressions of tenderness, his mind being fixed on going to Jerusalem and prepared for whatever awaited him. Expressions of tenderness among friends are proper, Barnes says, and tears may be inevitable at parting from those whom we love, but such expressions ought not to be allowed to interfere with the convictions of duty in their minds: if they have made up their minds that a certain course is proper and have resolved to pursue it, we ought neither to attempt to divert them from it nor to distract their minds by our remonstrances or our tears, but should resign them to their convictions with affection and prayer, yet with cheerfulness, lending them all the aid in our power and commending them to the blessing and protection of God. These remarks apply especially to those engaged in the missionary enterprise, Barnes says: it is trying to part with a son, a daughter or a beloved friend in order that they may go to proclaim the gospel to the benighted and dying heathen, and the act of parting for life, and the apprehension of the perils they may encounter on the ocean and in heathen lands, may be painful; but if they, like Paul, have looked at it calmly and candidly and with much prayer, and have come to the deliberate conclusion that it is the will of God, we ought not to weep and to break their hearts. We should cheerfully and confidently commit them to the protection of the God whom they serve, Barnes says, and remember that they are seeking his glory and that the parting of Christians, though for life, will be short: soon, in a better world, they will be united again to part no more, and the blessedness of that future meeting will be greatly heightened by all the sorrows and self-denials of separation here, and by all the benefits which such a separation may be the means of conveying to a dying world; that mother will meet with joy in heaven the son from whom, with many tears, she was sundered when he entered on a missionary life. His readiness to die was the true spirit of a martyr, Barnes says, and this spirit reigned in the hearts of all the early Christians. When he would not be persuaded to remain, they ceased remonstrating with him and urging him to remain, Barnes says: they were now assured that it was the will of God that he should go, and were now ready to submit to that will, which is an instance and an evidence of true piety, being the expression of a wish that whatever God might judge necessary for the advancement of his cause might take place, even though it should be attended with many trials; they commended their friend to the protection of God, confident that whatever should occur would be right. Charles Ellicott says the adjective for many days is in the comparative degree and implies a longer time than had been intended, probably because the voyage had been quicker than the travellers expected, so that there was time to remain at Caesarea and yet arrive at Jerusalem in time for Pentecost; there was at any rate time for the tidings of his arrival to reach Jerusalem, and for Agabus to come down in consequence. The manuscripts vary between his hands, that is Paul's, and his own, Ellicott says, but the latter is by far the best-supported reading; and it is interesting to note the revival of the old prophetic manner of predicting by symbolic acts, since Isaiah had walked naked and barefoot, Jeremiah had left his girdle in a cave on the banks of the Euphrates and had made bonds and yokes and put them on his neck, and Ezekiel had portrayed the siege of Jerusalem on a tile and cut the hair from his head and beard. Looking to the previous relations between Paul and Agabus at Antioch, Ellicott says, we may well believe that the latter, foreseeing the danger to which the Apostle would be exposed, came down to Caesarea in a spirit of friendly anxiety to warn him not to come, since the feeling which led to the murderous plot recorded later could be no secret to a prophet living at Jerusalem. For the first time the courage even of the Apostle's companions began to fail, Ellicott says, and Luke admits that he himself had joined in the entreaty: could not they, who were less known and therefore in less danger, go up without him, pay over the fund that had been collected among the Gentiles to James and the elders, and return to him at Caesarea? They of that place would of course include Philip and his daughters, Ellicott adds, and possibly, if he were still there, Cornelius and his friends; and they besought him, it will be noted, even with tears. The intense sensitiveness of Paul's nature shows itself in every syllable of his answer, Ellicott says: it was with no Stoic hardness that he resisted their entreaties, for they were positively crushing to him, and he adhered to his purpose, but it was as with a broken heart; in spite of this, however, his martyr-like, Luther-like nature carried him forward, since bonds and imprisonment were what he had heard of when he was yet at Corinth and Ephesus, before he had started on his journey, and what were they to one who was ready to face death? The pronouns are throughout emphatic, Ellicott notes: you are breaking my heart; I, for my part, am ready. It is perhaps too much to see in the closing words an acceptance of his purpose as being in accordance with the will of the Lord, Ellicott says: they were the natural expressions of resignation to what was seen to be inevitable, possibly used as a quotation from the prayer which the Lord had taught the disciples and which he had used himself. A.T. Robertson says the phrase for tarrying is a genitive absolute with an intensive preposition, and many days means more days than we expected; Agabus was a prophet like the daughters of Philip, mentioned already in connection with the famine predicted by him, but apparently not a man of prominence like Barnabas, and so there is no allusion to that former prophecy. There is a vivid use of three successive participles describing the dramatic action of Agabus, Robertson says, coming, taking and binding; the girdle is an old word, and his own feet and hands are the basis for the interpretation. Old Testament prophets often employed symbolic deeds, Robertson notes, and Jesus interpreted the symbolism of Peter's girding himself. Agabus was just from Jerusalem and probably knew the feeling there against Paul, Robertson says, and at any rate the Holy Spirit revealed it to him as he claims; the word for delivering is like the words of Jesus about himself, and he was delivered into the hands of the Gentiles and it took five years to get out of those hands. The verb for persuading is a conative imperfect, so that we tried to persuade him from going up, Robertson says; and Vincent cites the case of Regulus, who insisted on returning from Rome to Carthage to certain death, and that of Luther on the way to the Diet of Worms, where Spalatin begged Luther not to go on, and Luther said that though devils be as many in Worms as tiles upon the roofs, yet thither would he go. This dramatic warning of Agabus came on top of that at Tyre and Paul's own confession at Miletus, Robertson says, so that it is small wonder that Luke and the other messengers, together with Philip and his daughters, joined in a chorus of dissuasion to Paul. What are you doing weeping is a strong protest, Robertson says, and the verb for breaking the heart means to crush together, a late form of another meaning to break off, both vivid and expressive words, so as to enervate and unman one, weakening Paul's determination to go on with his duty; I am ready means I hold myself in readiness, and the negative used is the sharper one because of the contrast. Paul's readiness to die if need be at Jerusalem is like that of Jesus on the way to Jerusalem the last time, Robertson says, since even before that Luke said that he set his face to go on to Jerusalem, and later the disciples said to Jesus that the Jews were but now seeking to stone him, and goest thou thither; the stature of Paul rises here to heroic proportions for the name of the Lord Jesus. When he would not be persuaded is a genitive absolute, literally, he not being persuaded, Robertson says, and that was all: Paul's will was not broken, not even bent, and the verb for ceasing is an ingressive aorist of an old verb meaning to be quiet or silent. There is a quaint naivete in this confession by the friends of Paul, Robertson concludes: since Paul would not let them have their way, they were willing for the Lord to have his way, acquiescence after failure to have theirs.

Adam Clarke says Agabus was no doubt a prophet in the commonly received sense of the term, and his mode of acting was like that of the ancient prophets, who often accompanied their predictions with significant emblems: Jeremiah was commanded to bury his girdle by the river Euphrates to mark out the captivity of the Jews, and he refers the reader to more examples of this figurative or symbolical prophesying in Jeremiah, Isaiah and Ezekiel. The hands of the Gentiles means the Romans, Clarke says, for the Jews had not, properly speaking, the power of life and death; and as Agabus said he should be delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, he showed thereby that they would attempt to destroy his life, this prediction being literally fulfilled. They besought him not to go up to Jerusalem, Clarke says, for they all understood the prophecy to be conditional and contingent, and that it was in Paul's power to turn the scale. He was resolute and determined, Clarke says, but was under no constraining necessity; and when they said that the will of the Lord be done, they meant, may that which is most for his glory take place, since they plainly saw from the prophecy what would take place if Paul went to Jerusalem, and every one saw that he had power to go or not to go. John Wesley says that the nearer the event was, the more express were the predictions which prepared Paul for it. Binding his own feet and hands was in the manner that malefactors were wont to be bound when apprehended, Wesley says, and Paul's bonds were first particularly foretold at Caesarea, to which he afterward came in bonds. Both his fellow travellers and they of the place besought him not to go up to Jerusalem, Wesley says, but Paul knew that this prediction had the force of a command, and they did not know this. The apostles themselves were not void of human affections, Wesley says, and to him that is ready to die the burden is light. When he would not be persuaded, this was not obstinacy but true Christian resolution, Wesley concludes: we should never be persuaded either to do evil or to omit doing any good which is in our power, saying, the will of the Lord be done, which they were satisfied Paul knew.

debates: Whether the prophecy carried the force of a command: Wesley says Paul knew that it did and that his friends did not know this; Clarke says the opposite, that they all understood the prophecy to be conditional and contingent, that it lay in Paul's power to turn the scale, and that everyone saw he had power to go or not to go

What the company meant by submitting at last: Barnes takes it for true piety, the friends being now assured it was God's will and ready to submit; Calvin says they yielded lest they resist the Holy Spirit by whom they understood Paul to be governed; Ellicott thinks it too much to find in the words any acceptance of his purpose as the Lord's will, and calls them resignation to what was seen to be inevitable; Robertson finds a quaint naivete in the confession, since they were willing for the Lord to have his way only after failing to have their own

Why the warning was repeated a fourth time: Calvin says Paul had been more than sufficiently admonished already and that this was added for other men's sake, that they might know he entered the combat willingly; Wesley says only that the nearer the event, the more express the predictions; Ellicott supposes Agabus came down in friendly anxiety, knowing the feeling at Jerusalem

How the symbolic act should be read: Ellicott, Barnes and Clarke all take it as a revival of the old prophetic manner and give the same roll of precedents from Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel; Robertson turns instead to the Lord's own reading of Peter's girding; Calvin alone observes that false prophets afterwards aped the same technique, Zedekiah with his horns and Ananias in breaking Jeremiah's yoke
outliers: Calvin's remark that Satan is in a manner God's ape, and that the counterfeit signs of the false prophets imitate the true

Robertson's citation of Luther answering Spalatin that though the devils in Worms were as many as tiles upon the roofs, thither would he go, set beside Ellicott's calling Paul's nature Luther-like at the same verse
Ellicott's reconstruction of what the company were actually proposing, that the less conspicuous should carry the collected fund to Jerusalem and return to Paul at Caesarea
Robertson's note that the four prophetesses of the house joined the chorus of dissuasion against the prophet Agabus
Barnes's long application of the scene to modern missionary parting, and the mother who will meet in heaven the son from whom she was sundered with many tears
Robertson's observation that Paul was delivered into Gentile hands, in the very word used of Jesus, and took five years to get out of them

15.pericope_label: Taking up their baggage they go up to Jerusalem, lodging with Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, and the brethren receive them gladly

schools.summary: John Gill says they prepared themselves, both for their journey and for whatever trials and exercises they were to meet with, taking up their bundles, which hitherto had been brought by sea and were now put upon beasts, going by land from Caesarea. Certain of the disciples of Caesarea went with them, members of the church there, Gill says, and he adds the account of the pastors or bishops of that church as given by Reland: Theophilus, who was in the council held at Caesarea in the year one hundred and ninety-eight; Agricola, who subscribed in the council at Ancyra in the year three hundred and fourteen, though some do not acknowledge this Agricola but give the order after Theophilus as Theoctistus, Domnus, Theotecnus, Agapius and Eusebius, which last was in the council in Palestine in the year three hundred and eighteen and in the council at Nice in three hundred and twenty-five; Acacius, who succeeded him and was in a little council at Seleucia in three hundred and fifty-nine and another at Antioch in three hundred and sixty-three; Thalassius, who subscribed in the council at Constantinople in three hundred and eighty-one; Eulogius, or perhaps Euzoius, who was in the council at Diospolis in four hundred and fifteen; and Glyco, bishop of this church, who subscribed by Zozimus in the Chalcedon council held in four hundred and fifty-one, mention being also made of Irenaeus, who presided over it, in the acts of the same council. Then Paul and his companions came to Jerusalem, attended by the disciples of Caesarea and Mnason the old disciple with them, Gill says. John Calvin says Paul's companions declare that when they went about to call back Paul from danger they did rather care for the common safety of the Church than every man for his own life, for after they had taken the repulse they do not refuse to take part with him in the same danger; and yet this was a plausible excuse, that they were bound by no law to be hauled to suffer death through one man's stubbornness. This is truly to bring our affections in subjection to God, Calvin says, when we are terrified with no fear but every one of us endeavours, so much as he is able, to further that which we know does please him; and it appears more plainly what great ferventness of godliness was in the rest, who of their own accord accompany him and bring him a host, whereas notwithstanding they might well have feared many discommodities. Luke recites the glad reception, Calvin says, that he may set forth the equity of the brethren, who did not credit sinister rumours and false reports: though many envious and wicked men did daily, one after another, endeavour to bring Paul into contempt, yet because James and his fellows in office were well persuaded of his uprightness they were not estranged from him, and therefore they receive him now courteously and brotherly as a servant of Christ and declare that he is welcome. This moderation must we observe diligently, Calvin says, that we be not too hasty to believe wicked reports, especially when those who have given some testimony of their honesty, and whom we have experienced to serve God faithfully, are burdened with crimes unknown to us or else doubtful; because Satan knows that nothing is more fit to lay waste the kingdom of Christ than discord and disagreement among the faithful, he ceases not to spread abroad false speeches which may cause one to suspect another. Therefore we must shut our ears against false reports, Calvin concludes, that we may believe nothing concerning the faithful ministers of the Word but that which we know to be true.

Matthew Henry says that in these verses we have Paul's journey to Jerusalem from Caesarea and the company that went along with him. They took up their carriages, their bag and baggage, and as it should seem, like poor travellers or soldiers, were their own porters, Henry says, so little had they of change of raiment, and some think they had with them the money that was collected in the churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor saints at Jerusalem. If they could have persuaded Paul to go some other way they would gladly have gone along with him, Henry says, but since notwithstanding their dissuasion he will go to Jerusalem, they do not say, let him go by himself then, but as Thomas in a like case, when Christ would go into danger at Jerusalem, said, let us go and die with him; their resolution to cleave to Paul was like that of Ittai to cleave to David, that in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, there also will thy servant be, and thus Paul's boldness emboldened them. Certain of the disciples of Caesarea went along with them, Henry continues, and whether they designed to go however and took this opportunity of going with so much good company, or whether they went on purpose to see if they could do Paul any service and if possible prevent his trouble, or at least minister to him in it, does not appear; but the less while that Paul is likely to enjoy his liberty, the more industrious they are to improve every opportunity of conversation with him, as Elisha kept close to Elijah when he knew the time was at hand that he should be taken up. They brought with them an honest old gentleman that had a house of his own at Jerusalem in which he would gladly entertain Paul and his company, Henry says: such a great concourse of people there was to the feast that it was a hard matter to get lodgings, the public houses being taken up by those of the better sort, and it was looked upon as a scandalous thing for those that had private houses to let their rooms out at those times, but they must freely accommodate strangers with them; every one then would choose his friends to be his guests, and Mnason took Paul and his company to be his lodgers, though he had heard what trouble Paul was likely to come into, which might bring those that entertained him into trouble too, yet he shall be welcome to him, whatever comes of it. This Mnason is called an old disciple, a disciple from the beginning, Henry says, and some think one of the seventy disciples of Christ, or one of the first converts after the pouring out of the Spirit, or one of the first that was converted by the preaching of the gospel in Cyprus; however it was, it seems he had been long a Christian and was now in years. It is an honourable thing to be an old disciple of Jesus Christ, Henry says, to have been enabled by the grace of God to continue long in a course of duty, stedfast in the faith, and growing more and more prudent and experienced to a good old age; and with these old disciples one would choose to lodge, for the multitude of their years will teach wisdom.
