Many of the brethren at Jerusalem received him gladly, Henry says: as soon as they had notice that he was come to town they went to his lodgings at Mnason's house and congratulated him on his safe arrival, and told him they were glad to see him, and invited him to their houses, accounting it an honour to be known to one that was such an eminent servant of Christ; and Streso observes that the word here used concerning the welcome they gave to the apostles is used concerning the welcome of the apostles' doctrine earlier in this book.

Albert Barnes says that carriages is a most unhappy translation, since we apply the word now exclusively to a vehicle for conveying anything, as a coach, chariot, gig or cannon-carriage, while the original word means simply that they prepared themselves, made themselves ready, put their baggage in order and prepared for the journey. The English word carriage was formerly used in the sense of that which is carried, Barnes says, that is baggage, burden, vessels or furniture, and it was so used in the time that our translation was made, and in this sense it is to be understood where David left his carriage in the hand of the keeper of the carriage, and where at Michmash he laid up his carriages. The original in the next verse would be better translated that they brought them to Mnason of Cyprus, an old disciple, Barnes says: it is evident that though Mnason was originally of Cyprus he was now an inhabitant of Jerusalem and was well known to the disciples at Caesarea, and it is possible that he might have been at Caesarea and accompanied Paul to Jerusalem, but the more correct interpretation of the passage is that Paul and his fellow-travellers were conducted to his house in Jerusalem and that he was not with them in the journey. An old disciple means an early convert to Christianity, Barnes says, perhaps one who was converted before the crucifixion of the Saviour; with whom we should lodge means in whose house they were to take up their abode, the rites of hospitality having been shown in a distinguished manner by the early Christians. The brethren received them gladly, Barnes says, for they had been long absent, had been into distant regions and had encountered many dangers, so that it was a matter of joy that they had now returned in safety. Charles Ellicott says the rendering should be that they took up their baggage, the English word now used always of the vehicle that carries having been in common use at the time of the Authorised version for the things carried, the luggage or impedimenta of a traveller. So in the first book of Samuel David leaves his carriage, or as in the margin the vessels from upon him, in the hand of the keeper of the carriage, Ellicott says, and so in Udal's translation of Erasmus's Paraphrase of the New Testament the bearers of the paralytic are said to have taken their heavy carriage to the house-roof. Better, perhaps, an early disciple, Ellicott says of Mnason: the word for old refers less to personal age than to his having been a disciple from the beginning of the Church's history, and he may accordingly have been among those men of Cyprus who came to Antioch and were among the first to preach the gospel to the Gentiles. We may fairly infer that he was one of those who had been from the beginning among the eye-witnesses and ministers of the word to whom Luke refers as his informants, Ellicott says, and if so it is interesting as showing that our Lord's disciples were not limited to the natives of Galilee and Judaea. It lies on the surface of the narrative that Mnason had a house at Jerusalem in which he could receive Paul and his companions, Ellicott says, and the arrangement seems to have been made as the best course that could be taken to minimise the inevitable danger to which the Apostle was exposing himself: in that house at least he might be sure of personal safety, and the men from Caesarea would form a kind of escort as he went to and fro in the city. The reception was perhaps an informal welcome, Ellicott adds, given in Mnason's house by those who came there to receive the expected guests. A.T. Robertson says the participle for taking up baggage is a first aorist middle of an old verb meaning to furnish with things necessary, to pack up, which Ramsay holds means here to saddle horses, and that it occurs only here in the New Testament, while the verb for going up is an inchoative imperfect, we started to go up. The genitive for certain of the disciples occurs with a pronoun understood, as often in the Greek idiom, Robertson says, and the clause about Mnason is a thoroughly idiomatic Greek construction, the incorporation and attraction of the antecedent into the relative clause, so that Mnason is really the object of the participle for bringing but is placed in the clause after the relative and in the same locative case with it. He was originally from Cyprus but now in Caesarea, Robertson says; the Codex Bezae adds the words to a certain village and makes it mean that they were to lodge with Mnason at his home there about halfway to Jerusalem, and this may be true. The use of the word for old to mean early may refer to the fact that he was one of the original disciples at Pentecost, Robertson says, as Peter uses a like phrase of early days to refer to his experience at Caesarea; and he quotes Furneaux that as the number of the first disciples lessened, the next generation accorded a sort of honour to the survivors. The phrase for their coming is a genitive absolute again, Robertson says, the verb for receiving is an old compound found only in Luke in the New Testament, and the adverb for gladly occurs here only in the New Testament; perhaps this first glad welcome was from Paul's personal friends in Jerusalem.

Adam Clarke says they made themselves ready, packed up their things and got their baggage in order, and that this is what the text means. It is not very likely that they would bring a man with them with whom they were to lodge in Jerusalem, Clarke says, and therefore the text should perhaps be read as Bishop Patrick proposes, that there went with them certain of the disciples of Caesarea, bringing them to one Mnason with whom they were to lodge, which is most likely, as the text will bear this translation. But it is possible that Mnason, formerly of Cyprus and now an inhabitant of Jerusalem, might have been down at Caesarea, met the disciples and invited them to lodge with him while they were at Jerusalem, and, having transacted his business at Caesarea, might now accompany them to Jerusalem, Clarke allows. His being an old disciple may either refer to his having been a very early convert, probably one of those on the day of Pentecost, or to his being now an old man, Clarke says. John Wesley says they took up their baggage, which probably went by sea before, and that what they took with them now in particular was the alms they were carrying to Jerusalem. The disciples brought them to one Mnason, a Cyprian, an old disciple, Wesley says: he was a native of Cyprus but an inhabitant of Jerusalem, and probably one of the first converts there.

debates: Where Mnason was met and where he lived: Barnes holds the sentence better rendered that they were brought to Mnason at Jerusalem, and that he did not travel with them; Clarke thinks it unlikely they would bring along the man with whom they were to lodge and prefers Bishop Patrick's rendering, while allowing that Mnason may have come down and returned with them; Robertson reports the addition in Codex Bezae of the words to a certain village, which would make the lodging a house halfway up, and judges it may be true; Gill and Henry have him travelling in the party

What an old disciple means: Ellicott prefers early to old and refers the word to standing rather than age, making him possibly one of the men of Cyprus who first preached to Gentiles at Antioch and one of Luke's own informants; Barnes guesses at a convert made before the crucifixion; Clarke offers either a convert of Pentecost or simply an aged man; Henry reports the opinion that he was one of the seventy

What the welcome at Jerusalem was: Barnes reads plain joy at a safe return from distant regions and many dangers; Ellicott and Robertson both take it as informal and private, given by personal friends before the formal reception that follows; Calvin makes it evidence that James and his colleagues refused to credit the rumours daily spread against Paul

Why the lodging was arranged as it was: Ellicott reads it as a precaution, the house securing personal safety and the men from Caesarea forming a kind of escort; Henry explains it by the crowding of the feast, when the public houses were taken and it was thought scandalous to let private rooms for money
outliers: Ellicott's inference that Mnason was among the eye-witnesses from the beginning whom Luke names as his informants, and that the Lord's disciples were therefore not limited to Galilee and Judaea
Furneaux's remark, quoted by Robertson, that as the first disciples grew fewer the next generation accorded a sort of honour to the survivors
Calvin's observation that the companions might plausibly have pleaded that no law bound them to be hauled to death through one man's stubbornness, and that they went anyway
Gill's catalogue of the later bishops of Caesarea from Reland, running from Theophilus in the second century to the council of Chalcedon
Ellicott's citation of Udal's version of Erasmus, where the bearers of the paralytic take their heavy carriage to the house-roof
Henry's comparison of the companions to Ittai cleaving to David and to Elisha keeping close to Elijah when the time of his taking up drew near

18.pericope_label: Paul goes in with the company to James, all the elders being present, and rehearses one by one what God had wrought among the Gentiles

schools.summary: John Gill says this was the day following after they were come into Jerusalem, and that Paul saluted James and the elders with him, which was either done by a kiss, as the Arabic version adds, or by asking of their health and wishing a continuance of it and all prosperity to attend them. John Calvin says we may gather from this place what we had already in the fifteenth chapter, that so often as any weighty business was to be handled the elders were wont to come together, to the end the consultation might be more quiet without the multitude; and we shall see anon that the people were likewise admitted in their order, yet after the elders had had their more private consultation among themselves. Now Paul shows his modesty, Calvin says, when he does not make himself the author of those things which he had done but, giving the praise to God, calls himself only the minister whose agency God had used; as we must grant that whatsoever thing is excellent and worthy of praise is not done by our own power, but forasmuch as God works in us, and especially touching the edifying of the Church. Again it appears how far off the elders were from envy, Calvin says, when they glorify God for the joyful success. But because mention is made of no other apostle besides James, Calvin continues, we may conjecture that they were gone into diverse places to spread abroad and preach the gospel as their calling did require, for the Lord had not appointed them to stay still at Jerusalem, but after they had made a beginning there he commanded them to go into Judea and other parts of the world. The error of those men who think that James was one of the disciples whom Paul numbers among the three pillars of the Church is refuted before in the fifteenth chapter, Calvin says; and though the same commandment was given to him which was given to the rest of his fellows in office, yet he does not doubt but that they did so divide themselves that James stood still at Jerusalem, whither many strangers were wont daily to resort, for that was all one as if he had preached the gospel far and wide in remote places. This speech has two members, Calvin says: first the elders say that so many of the Jews as were converted, seeing they are earnest followers of the law, are evil affected towards Paul, because they think that he endeavours with might and main to abolish the law; and secondly they exhort him that, making a solemn vow, he purge himself, that he may not be had in suspicion any longer. They object to Paul the multitude of believers, Calvin says, that he may the more willingly yield to them, for if they had been a few stubborn fellows he would not have been so much moved, but now he may not neglect both much people and the whole body of the church.

Matthew Henry says Paul ascribed all his success to God, and to God they gave the praise: God had honoured him more than any of the apostles, yet they did not envy him but on the contrary glorified the Lord, and they could not do more to encourage Paul to go on cheerfully in his work. James and the elders of the church at Jerusalem asked Paul to gratify the believing Jews by some compliance with the ceremonial law, Henry says, and they thought it was prudent in him to conform thus far; it was great weakness to be so fond of the shadows when the substance was come, for the religion Paul preached tended not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, since he preached Christ, the end of the law for righteousness, and repentance and faith, in which we are to make great use of the law. The weakness and evil of the human heart strongly appear, Henry says, when we consider how many even of the disciples of Christ had not due regard to the most eminent minister that ever lived: not the excellence of his character, nor the success with which God blessed his labours, could gain their esteem and affection, seeing that he did not render the same respect as themselves to mere ceremonial observances; how watchful should we be against prejudices. The apostles were not free from blame in all they did, Henry says, and it would be hard to defend Paul from the charge of giving way too much in this matter; it is vain to attempt to court the favour of zealots, or bigots to a party, and this compliance of Paul did not answer, for the very thing by which he hoped to pacify the Jews provoked them and brought him into trouble. But the all-wise God overruled both their advice and Paul's compliance with it to serve a better purpose than was intended, Henry says: it was in vain to think of pleasing men who would be pleased with nothing but the rooting out of Christianity, and integrity and uprightness will be more likely to preserve us than insincere compliances; and it should warn us not to press men to do what is contrary to their own judgment to oblige us.

Albert Barnes says this was James the Less, who resided at Jerusalem, and that it is not improbable he was the only one of the apostles then there, since there is reason to believe that the church at Jerusalem was left under his particular care; it was natural therefore that Paul and his travelling companions should take an early opportunity to see him. James was the cousin of our Lord, Barnes says, and is called the Lord's brother, so that on all accounts he was entitled to and would receive particular respect from the early disciples. Paul saluted them with the usual tokens of respect and affection, Barnes says, and declared particularly what God had wrought as an evidence that God had been with him; it is not improbable that there might have been some suspicion in regard to Paul among the disciples at Jerusalem, and he might have heard that they were prejudiced against him, and this prejudice would be removed by his stating what had actually occurred under his ministry. Charles Ellicott says that, looking to the earlier statement of Paul's purpose, it seems natural to infer that this was on or near the Day of Pentecost, when the city would be crowded with pilgrims and the Church would be holding its solemn festival, not without memories of the great gifts of the Spirit and prayers for their renewal. The Bishop of Jerusalem, to give him the title which, though apparently not then borne by him, expressed his functions and was afterwards attached to his name, was there with the elders of the Church, Ellicott says, and Luke is careful to add that they were all there; on their part there was no reluctance to receive the Apostle of the Gentiles into full fellowship. The rendering should be one by one, or in detail, Ellicott says, the adverb of the Authorised version having acquired in modern English a slightly different meaning; and this must obviously have implied a narrative of considerable length, including an outline of all that had passed since the earlier visit and ending with an account of the contribution which he and his companions had brought with them from well-nigh all the churches of the Gentiles. A.T. Robertson says the verb for going in is an imperfect of an old classic verb used only four times in the New Testament, a mark of the literary style rather than the colloquial use of the commoner word. So then Luke is present, Robertson says, the next use of we being at the departure for Rome, but it is not likely that Luke was away from Paul in Jerusalem and Caesarea, since the reports of what was done and said in both places are so full and minute that it seems reasonable that Luke got first hand information here, and there are many details that read like an eyewitness's story. It was probably the house of James, Robertson says, and clearly James is the leading elder while the others are his guests in a formal reception to Paul; it is noticeable that the apostles are not mentioned though both elders and apostles are named at the Conference in the fifteenth chapter, so that it would seem the apostles are away on preaching tours, and the whole church was not called together probably because of the known prejudice against Paul created by the Judaizers. The verb for rehearsing is an imperfect middle of an old verb meaning to lead out or to draw out in narrative, Robertson says, so that Paul is pictured as taking his time, for he had a great story to tell of what had happened since they saw him last; the phrase means according to each one, and the aorist for what God had wrought is a summary constative that gathers up all that God did, Paul taking pains to give God the glory. It is possible that at this formal meeting Paul observed an absence of warmth and enthusiasm in contrast with the welcome accorded by his friends the day before, Robertson says, and Furneaux thinks that Paul was coldly received on this day in spite of the generous offering brought from the Gentile Christians, since it looks as though his misgiving as to its reception was confirmed, nor do we hear that the Christians of Jerusalem later put in so much as a word on his behalf with either the Jewish or the Roman authorities, or expressed any sympathy with him during his long imprisonment at Caesarea. The most that can be said is that the Judaizers referred to by James do not appear actively against him, Robertson concludes, since the collection and the plan proposed by James accomplished that much at any rate, and it stopped the mouths of those lions.

John Chrysostom says this was the Bishop of Jerusalem, and to him Paul is sent on an earlier occasion; this James was brother of the Lord, a great and admirable man. Mark the Bishop's unassuming behaviour, Chrysostom says, and that the elders were present. Again Paul relates to them the things relating to the Gentiles, not indulging in vainglory, God forbid, but wishing to show forth the mercy of God and to fill them with great joy, Chrysostom says: see accordingly that when they heard it they glorified God, and did not praise nor admire Paul, for in such wise had he narrated, as referring all to Him. Observe with what modest deference they too speak, Chrysostom continues: they said to him, and James does not as Bishop discourse authoritatively, but they take Paul as partner with them in their view, saying, thou seest, brother, as though immediately and at the outset apologising for themselves and saying, we did not wish this, seest thou the necessity of the thing. They say not how many thousands we have made catechumens, but how many there are, Chrysostom notes, and that these are all zealous for the law; and here are two reasons, the number of them and their views, for neither had they been few would it have been right to despise them, nor if they were many and did not all cling to the law would there have been need to make much account of them. Then a third cause is given, Chrysostom says, that they all have been informed of thee: they say not that they have heard, but that so they have believed and have been taught, that thou teachest apostasy from Moses to all the Jews which are among the Gentiles. They say these things as advising, not as commanding, Chrysostom observes: make thy defence in act, not in word, that all may know that those things whereof they were informed concerning thee are nothing, but that thou thyself also walkest orderly and keepest the law; and they say not teachest, but, of superabundance, that thou thyself also keepest the law, for of course the matter of chief interest was not whether he did not teach others but that he did himself observe the law. What then, he might say, if the Gentiles should learn it, shall I not injure them, Chrysostom asks; and the answer is that even we, the teachers of the Jews, have sent unto them, so that as we commanded them, although we are preachers to the Jews, so do thou, although a preacher to the Gentiles, cooperate with us. Observe Paul, Chrysostom says: he does not say, well, but I can bring forward Timothy whom I circumcised, well, but I can satisfy them by what I have to say of myself; but he complied and did all, for in fact thus was it expedient to do, since it was one thing to take effectual measures for clearing himself and another to have done these things without the knowledge of any of the parties, and it was a step open to no suspicion, the fact of his even bearing the expenses.

Adam Clarke says this was James the Less, son of Mary and cousin to our Lord, who appears to have been bishop of the Church in Jerusalem and perhaps the only apostle who continued in that city, and we have already seen what a very important character he sustained in the council. All the elders were present, Clarke says, and it appears that they had been convened about matters of serious and important moment, some thinking it was relative to Paul himself, of whose arrival they had heard, and they well knew how many of those that believed were disaffected towards him. He no doubt had heard that they were prejudiced against him, Clarke says, and by declaring what God had done by him among the Gentiles he showed how groundless this prejudice was, for were he a bad man, or doing anything that he should not do, God would not have made him such a singular instrument of so much good. John Wesley says Paul went in with them that it might appear they were all of one mind, to James, commonly called the Lord's brother, the only apostle then presiding over the Churches in Judea.

debates: How Paul was received at the formal meeting: Ellicott says there was no reluctance to receive the Apostle of the Gentiles into full fellowship and that Luke is careful to note they were all there; Robertson raises the opposite possibility of an absence of warmth, and quotes Furneaux that Paul's misgiving about the collection looks to have been confirmed and that the Jerusalem Christians never afterwards spoke a word for him with either authority; Calvin and Henry read the elders as free from envy

Whether Paul was right to comply: Chrysostom says he did not plead Timothy's circumcision or argue his case but complied and did all, since so it was expedient, and that bearing the expenses left the step open to no suspicion; Henry says it would be hard to defend him from the charge of giving way too much, that it is vain to court the favour of zealots, and that integrity would more likely have preserved him than insincere compliance

Why only James is named: Calvin conjectures the other apostles had gone abroad to preach as their calling required, James remaining where strangers daily resorted, which was as good as preaching far and wide; Robertson makes the same inference from their absence at a meeting where the earlier council had named both apostles and elders

Why the elders met apart from the church: Calvin says weighty business was always handled first by the elders, that the consultation might be quieter without the multitude, the people being admitted after; Robertson supposes the whole church was not called because of the known prejudice against Paul created by the Judaizers
outliers: Chrysostom's reading of the elders as apologising at the outset, saying in effect that they did not wish this and that Paul should see the necessity of the thing
Chrysostom's note that they claim no credit, saying not how many thousands we have made catechumens but only how many there are
Furneaux's observation, quoted by Robertson, that no Jerusalem Christian is recorded to have expressed sympathy with Paul during his long imprisonment at Caesarea
Ellicott's caution that the title of bishop expressed James's functions but was apparently not then borne by him
Chrysostom's summary of the counsel as a defence to be made in act and not in word
Robertson's judgement that the collection and the plan proposed stopped the mouths of those lions

20.pericope_label: James reports the myriads of believing Jews zealous for the law, and the charge that Paul teaches apostasy from Moses

schools.summary: John Gill says that when they heard the narrative of the wonderful spread of the Gospel among the Gentiles and the numerous conversions of them, they glorified God; that they are informed of thee means by persons that came from the several parts of the Gentile world where the apostle had been preaching, and by letters which came from the Jews in those parts, who were no friends to the apostle's ministry. What is it therefore, Gill says, means, is it true or not, or what must be done in this case, what method must be taken to remove these objections and reconcile the minds of the people; and the multitude must needs come together means either the whole church at Jerusalem or the great confluence of people, even of believing Jews, that were come from all parts thither, since there is no hindering of their coming together to see the apostle and to hear what he has to say to the objections against him and complaints of him. John Calvin says the verb is a verb neuter, as if they should say, the multitude must of necessity come together, for it had been an absurd thing that an apostle of such rare report should not come before the whole multitude of the faithful, since if he had eschewed the light and sight of people the sinister suspicion might have been increased. Nevertheless we see how modestly the elders behaved themselves in nourishing concord, Calvin says, when they prevent the offence of the people in time, saving that they bear too much peradventure with their infirmity in requiring a vow of Paul. But this moderation must be kept in the Church, Calvin says, that the pastors be in great authority and yet that they rule not proudly as lords, neither despise the rest of the body; for the distinction of orders, which is the bond of peace, ought not to be any cause of dissension.

Albert Barnes says they gave praise to the Lord for what he had done, seeing new proofs of his goodness and mercy and rendering him thanks for all that had been accomplished, and that there was no jealousy that it had been done by the instrumentality of Paul, since true piety will rejoice in the spread of the gospel and in the conversion of sinners by whatever instrumentality it may be effected. The language of tenderness in the address, recognising Paul as a fellow-labourer and fellow Christian, implies a wish that Paul would do all that could be done to avoid giving offence and to conciliate the favour of his countrymen, Barnes says. The number of converts at this time must have been very great, Barnes continues: twenty-five years before this, three thousand had been converted at one time, and afterwards the number had swelled to some more thousands, so that the assertion that there were then many thousands implies that the work so signally begun on the day of Pentecost had not ceased and that many more had been converted to the Christian faith. They are spoken of as believers or as having faith in Christ, in contradistinction from those who rejected him and whose characteristic trait it was that they were unbelievers, Barnes says, and they still observe the law of Moses, the reference being to the law respecting circumcision, sacrifices, distinctions of meats and days, and festivals. It may seem remarkable that they should still continue to observe those rites, Barnes says, since it was the manifest design of Christianity to abolish them, but we are to remember that those rites had been appointed by God and that they were trained to their observance; that the apostles conformed to them while they remained in Jerusalem and did not deem it best to set themselves violently against them; that the question about their observance had never been agitated at Jerusalem, but only among the Gentile converts, where it must arise, for if they were to be observed they must have been imposed upon them by authority; and that the decision of the council related only to the Gentile converts and did not touch the question whether those rites were to be observed by the Jewish converts. Reports respecting the conduct of Paul would be likely to be in circulation among all at Jerusalem, Barnes says, since his remarkable conversion, his distinguished zeal and his success among the Gentiles would make his conduct a subject of special interest; evil-minded men among the Jews who came up to Jerusalem from the different places where he had been would be likely to represent him as the decided enemy of the laws of Moses, and these reports would be likely to reach the ears of the Jewish converts, and, as they gained ground, would be greatly magnified until suspicion might be excited among the Christians at Jerusalem. From all the evidence which we have of his conduct this report was incorrect and slanderous, Barnes says: the truth appears to have been that he did not enjoin the observance of those laws on the Gentile converts, that the effect of his ministry on them was to lead them to suppose that their observance was not necessary, and that he argued with the Jews themselves, where it could be done, against the obligation of those laws and customs since the Messiah had come, they having depended on that observance for justification and salvation, which Paul strenuously opposed and defended at length in the epistles he wrote. Yet these facts might be easily misunderstood and perverted, Barnes says, so as to give rise to the slanderous report that he was everywhere the enemy of Moses and the law; and the word customs denotes the rites of the Mosaic economy, the offering of sacrifices, incense, the oblations, anointings and festivals which the law of Moses prescribed. What is it therefore means what is to be done, what is it proper to do to avoid the effects of the evil report which has been circulated, Barnes says; and the multitude must needs come together means there will inevitably be a tumultuous assemblage which it will be impossible to prevent, the reasons being that their minds were exceedingly agitated that one of their own countrymen had, as they understood, been advising apostasy from the religion of their fathers, that it had been extensively done in many parts of the world and with great success, and that Paul, having as they believed himself apostatised from the national religion, had become very conspicuous, so that his very presence in Jerusalem would be likely to excite a tumult. It was therefore the part of friendship to him and to the cause to devise some proper plan to prevent, if possible, the anticipated excitement, Barnes concludes. Charles Ellicott says the better manuscripts give that they glorified God, and that the tense implies continued action, so that although its meaning would be satisfied by assuming mere ejaculations of wonder and praise, it is at least not improbable that there was a more formal thanksgiving. The phrase is literally how many myriads, that is tens of thousands, Ellicott says: the numbers seem large if we think of the population of Jerusalem only, but the crowds that came from all quarters to the Feast of Pentecost would fully justify the statement; the speaker here is obviously James as the president of the assembly, and there is no trace of the presence of any of the Apostles. Better, the word being a substantive and not an adjective, zealots for the law, Ellicott says, the term having been an almost technical one for the most rigid class of Pharisees, as Paul describes himself in this sense a zealot. This, it is clear, was the current version of Paul's teaching, Ellicott says, and we may ask how far it was a true representation of its tendencies: as a personal accusation it was of course easy to refute, since his rule of adaptation led him to be to the Jews as a Jew, he taught that every man, circumcised or uncircumcised, should accept his position with its attendant obligations, he had himself taken the Nazarite vow and had circumcised Timothy, and it was probably false that he had ever taught that Jews ought not to circumcise their children. But fanaticism is sometimes clear-sighted in its bitterness, Ellicott continues, and the Judaisers felt that when it was proclaimed that circumcision was nothing in its bearing on man's relations to God, it ceased to have a reason for existing and sank to the level of a mere badge of the national exclusiveness, which in its turn was assailed by Paul's teaching that all middle walls of partition were broken down and that Jews and Gentiles were alike one in Christ. If a Jew had asked, why then should I circumcise my child, it would not have been easy to return a satisfying answer, Ellicott says: if it were said, to avoid giving offence, that was clearly only temporary and local in its application, and the practice would die out as people ceased to be offended; if it were urged that it was a divine command, there was the reply that as a command it had been virtually though not formally repealed when the promises and privileges connected with it were withdrawn, since it was the seal of a covenant and could hardly be looked upon as binding when the covenant itself had been superseded. Few Christians would now hold that a converted Jew was still bound to circumcise, as well as baptise, his children, Ellicott says, and the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews did but push Paul's teaching to its legitimate conclusions when he said that the new covenant had made the first old and that what is decaying and waxing old is ready to vanish away. Literally it is that thou teachest apostasy from Moses, Ellicott notes, the term used, with all its burden of evil import, adding weight to the charge. More accurately the next clause is, at all events a crowd must needs come together, Ellicott says: the report of Paul's arrival was sure to spread, and those who heard of it would be eager to see how he acted, and whether he would ostentatiously reproduce in Jerusalem that living as a Greek with Greeks of which they heard as his manner at Corinth and Ephesus; the advice which followed was intended to allay the suspicion of the timid and to disappoint the expectations of more determined adversaries. A.T. Robertson says the verb for glorifying is an inchoative imperfect, they began to glorify God, though without special praise of Paul, and that the word for thousands is the old word for ten thousand and then an indefinite number like our myriads. It is a surprising statement even with allowable hyperbole, Robertson says, but one may recall the earlier numbers in this book; there were undoubtedly a great many thousands of believers in Jerusalem and all Jewish Christians, some, alas, Judaizers, and this list may include the Christians from neighbouring towns in Palestine and even some from foreign countries here at the Feast of Pentecost, but we do not have to count the hostile Jews from Asia, who were clearly not Christians at all. Zealots is a substantive rather than an adjective with an objective genitive, Robertson says, the word being from a verb meaning to burn with zeal or to boil, while the Greeks used it for an imitator or admirer; there was a party of Zealots developed from the Pharisees, a group of what would be called hot-heads, who brought on the war with Rome, and one of this party was in the number of the twelve apostles. It is important to understand the issues in Jerusalem, Robertson says: it was settled at the Jerusalem Conference that the Mosaic ceremonial law was not to be imposed upon Gentile Christians, and Paul won freedom for them, but it was not said that it was wrong for Jewish Christians to go on observing it if they wished, and we have seen Paul observing the passover at Philippi and planning to reach Jerusalem for Pentecost. The Judaizers rankled under Paul's victory and power in spreading the gospel among the Gentiles and gave him great trouble in Galatia and Corinth, Robertson says, and they were busy against him in Jerusalem also, so that it was to undo the harm done by them there that Paul gathered the great collection from the Gentile Christians and brought it with him and the delegates from the churches; clearly then Paul had real ground for his apprehension of trouble while still in Corinth, and the repeated warnings along the way were amply justified. The verb for being informed means to sound down, to resound, to re-echo, to teach orally, Robertson says, and oriental students today often study aloud; this oral teaching about Paul was done diligently by the Judaizers who had raised trouble against Peter and Paul, and having failed in their attacks on Paul's world campaigns they now try to undermine him at home, having had a free hand in his long absence and great success in prejudicing the Jerusalem Christians against him. So James, in the presence of the other elders and probably at their suggestion, feels called upon to tell Paul the actual situation, Robertson says; the dreadful word is apostasy, a late form, and Furneaux remarks that in the eyes of the church at Jerusalem this was a far more serious matter than the previous question at the Conference about the status of Gentile converts. Here it is not the Judaizers but the elders of the church with James as their spokesman on behalf of the church as a whole, Robertson says: they do not believe this false charge, but they wish Paul to set it straight, and Paul had made his position clear in his epistles for all who cared to know. The construction is not indirect assertion but indirect command, Robertson says, so that the point is not that Paul stated what the Jewish Christians in the dispersion do, but that he says they are not to go on circumcising their children; Paul taught the very opposite and had Timothy circumcised because he was half Jew and half Greek, his own practice being to the Jews as a Jew. The charge was here enlarged to cover the whole custom and to make Paul out an enemy of Jewish life and teachings, Robertson says, and that same charge had been made against Stephen when young Saul was the leader, that he will change the customs which Moses delivered unto us, so that it actually seemed that some of the Jews cared more for Moses than for God. What is it therefore means what is to be done about it, Robertson says: clearly James and the elders do not believe these misrepresentations of Paul's teaching, but many do, and there was no way to conceal Paul's arrival nor was it wise to do so; and two of the uncials with several cursives omit the clause that the multitude must needs come together.

Adam Clarke says the phrase means how many myriads, how many times ten thousand, which intimates that there had been a most extraordinary and rapid work even among the Jews; but what is here spoken is not to be confined to the Jews of Jerusalem, but to all that had come from different parts of the land to be present at this Pentecost. The Jewish economy was not yet destroyed, Clarke says, nor had God as yet signified that the whole of its observances were done away: he continued to tolerate that dispensation, which was to be in a certain measure in force till the destruction of Jerusalem, and from that period it was impossible for them to observe their own ritual; thus God abolished the Mosaic dispensation by rendering, in the course of his providence, the observance of it impossible. From anything that appears in the course of this book to the contrary, the information that Paul taught men to forsake Moses was incorrect, Clarke says: we do not find Paul preaching thus to the Jews, and it is true that in his epistles, some of which had been written before this time, he showed that circumcision and uncircumcision were equally unavailable for the salvation of the soul and that by the deeds of the law no man could be justified, but he had not yet said to any Jew, forsake Moses and do not circumcise your children. He told them that Jesus Christ had delivered them from the yoke of the law, Clarke says, but they had as yet liberty to wear that yoke if they pleased; he had shown them that their ceremonies were useless but not destructive, and that they were only dangerous when they depended on them for salvation, and this is the sum of what Paul had taught on this subject. Whether the coming together of the multitude refers to a regular convocation of the Church or to a tumult that would infallibly take place when it was heard that the apostle was come, we cannot pretend to say, Clarke adds, but it is evident that James and the elders wished some prudent steps to be taken in order to prevent an evil that they had too much reason to fear. John Wesley says they were all zealous for the whole Mosaic dispensation, and asks how astonishing this is: did none of the apostles beside Paul know that this dispensation was now abolished, and if they did both know and testify this, how came their hearers not to believe them. They have been informed concerning thee that thou teachest the Jews not to circumcise their children nor to walk after the customs of the Mosaic law, Wesley says, and so undoubtedly he did, and so he wrote to all the Churches in Galatia, among whom were many Jews; yea, and James himself had long before assented to Peter, affirming before all the apostles and all the brethren that this very law was a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear. Amazing, Wesley exclaims, that they did not know this, or that if they did, they did not openly testify it at all hazards to every Jewish convert in Jerusalem. What is it therefore means what is to be done, Wesley says, and the multitude will certainly gather together in a tumultuous manner unless they be some way pacified.

debates: Whether the report about Paul was true: Wesley says flatly that it was, that Paul did so teach and so wrote to the Galatians, and marvels that the apostles did not know or would not testify that the law was a yoke none could bear; Clarke, of the same school, says the information was incorrect and that Paul had never told any Jew to forsake Moses; Barnes calls it incorrect and slanderous; Robertson says the elders themselves did not believe it; Ellicott holds it false as a personal accusation but grants that the Judaisers were clear-sighted about its tendency, since once circumcision was declared nothing no satisfying reason for it remained

What the necessary gathering of the crowd means: Barnes takes it as an inevitable tumult the elders were trying to forestall, and Wesley as a tumultuous assembly unless the people are pacified; Clarke will not decide between a regular convocation and a riot; Calvin reads the necessity positively, that an apostle of such report must appear before the whole multitude, since shunning the sight of the people would have deepened suspicion; Robertson reports that two uncials and several cursives omit the clause

Why Jewish believers still kept the law: Barnes answers that the rites were of divine appointment, that the apostles conformed while at Jerusalem, that the question had only ever been raised about Gentile converts, and that the council's decision touched those converts only; Clarke answers providentially, that God tolerated the dispensation until the destruction of Jerusalem made its observance impossible; Robertson notes that the Conference left Jewish Christians free to observe it if they wished

How large the number was: Ellicott and Clarke both explain the myriads by the pilgrim crowds rather than the resident population; Robertson calls the figure surprising even as hyperbole and excludes the hostile Asian Jews from the count; Barnes traces a continuous increase from the three thousand of Pentecost
outliers: Ellicott's concession that fanaticism is sometimes clear-sighted in its bitterness, and his admission that few Christians now would hold a converted Jew bound to circumcise as well as baptise his children
Wesley's exclamation that it is amazing the apostles did not know the dispensation abolished, or did not testify it at all hazards to every Jewish convert in Jerusalem
Robertson's note that the word for being informed means to teach by sound, and that oriental students still study aloud
Furneaux's judgement, quoted by Robertson, that this charge was in Jerusalem eyes a graver matter than the earlier question about the status of Gentile converts
Robertson's observation that the same charge of changing the customs had been laid against Stephen when young Saul was the leader
Calvin's caution that the elders, in requiring a vow of Paul, perhaps bore too indulgently with the people's infirmity

23.pericope_label: James counsels Paul to purify himself with four men under a vow and pay their charges, and Paul takes them and enters the temple

schools.summary: John Gill says the counsel is given not as commanding but as advising, and not as to what was a duty and necessary as such, but as a point of prudence; that to purify himself with them means to join himself to them and make one of their number, attending to the rules prescribed to a Nazarite, who is to be holy to the Lord. The words about the Gentiles are added to show that the Jews were not offended with Paul for not insisting on the circumcision of the believing Gentiles, Gill says, and to remove an objection that Paul might make, that should he comply with this advice and the believing Gentiles hear of it, it might be a stumblingblock and a snare to them, who by his example might think themselves obliged to regard the law; and Beza's ancient copy adds the words, they have nothing to say to thee. Then Paul took the four men that had the vow on them, Gill says, joined himself to them and put himself in the same condition and under a like vow: this he did, not as what he thought himself bound to do in obedience to the law, and much less as necessary to salvation, but to satisfy weak minds and remove their prejudices, that he might gain them and be useful to them; and in such a case he would very easily and readily condescend, but when such things were insisted on as points of duty, and especially when urged as necessary to salvation, no one more stiffly opposed them. John Calvin says the elders seem to have fallen into a foolish indulgence through too much love of their nation, but that a clear judgment on the case depends upon circumstances which are hid from us at this day, though they knew them well: the whole body almost consisted of Jews, so that they needed not fear offending the Gentiles, whereas in other regions this was the cause of dissension, because every man was wedded to his own custom and would prescribe a law to others. Furthermore they had at Jerusalem many things which might provoke them to keep the ceremonies of the law, Calvin says, so that they had a greater excuse if they forsook them more slowly; and though their zeal were not void of fault, yet as it was a hard matter to reform it, so it could not be done of a sudden, since we see how this superstition was scarcely in long time pulled from the apostles, and because new disciples came daily unto the faith the infirmity was nourished in all together. Yet we must not deny but that ignorance was coupled with obstinacy, Calvin says, which the elders nevertheless tolerated lest they should do more hurt by using violent remedies; and though these four be reckoned among the faithful, yet their vow was superstitious, whereby it appears that the apostles had much trouble in that nation, which was not only hardened in the worship of the law through long use but was also naturally malapert and almost intractable. It may be that these men were as yet but novices, Calvin allows, and therefore their faith was yet but slender, wherefore the doctors suffered them to perform the vow which they had unadvisedly made. As touching Paul, because he made this vow not moved thereunto by his own conscience but for their sakes, with whose error he did bear, the case stood otherwise with him, Calvin says; notwithstanding, we must see whether this were one of the indifferent ceremonies which the faithful might omit or keep at their pleasure, and it seems indeed to have in it certain things which ill accorded with the profession of faith. But because the end thereof was thanksgiving, and there was nothing in the rite itself repugnant to the faith of Christ, Paul did not doubt to descend thus far to make his religion known, Calvin says: therefore Paul did that which he says of himself elsewhere, because he made himself a companion of those which followed the law as if he himself were in subjection to the law, and finally he was made all things to all men that he might win all, yet so that he might pollute himself with no sacrilege under a colour of love. They seem to persuade Paul to dissemble, Calvin continues, for the rumour rose not upon nothing that he did call away the Jews from the ceremonies; but it was sufficient for Paul and the elders if they could remove the slander which was unjustly raised, that he was an apostate from the law, and there might a better opportunity be offered shortly, that in purging himself he might call them back by little and little from their error. Neither was it good or profitable that Paul should be counted an observer of the law any long time, as the disciples were then commonly, Calvin says, for by this means a thicker veil should have been put before their eyes to darken the light of Christ; wherefore let us know that Paul did not dissemble, but sincerely professed that he did not hate the law but rather thought reverently of it, and they will him to bestow cost together with them because they were wont to put their money together that they might offer sacrifice together. They add the words about the Gentiles lest they be thought to go about to take away that liberty which they had granted, Calvin says; but in the meanwhile they seem to keep the Jews in bondage, from which they set free the Gentiles alone in plain words. He answers that forasmuch as the estate of all was alike, like liberty was granted to both, but there is mention made of the Jews, who were so addicted to their observations and ceremonies that they would not take to themselves that liberty which they might well challenge, while the apostles did by name provide for the Gentiles lest the Jews, after their wonted custom, should reject them as profane and unclean. Whereas some accuse Paul of craftiness, as if he did play the hypocrite, Calvin says he has before refuted this, yet does not deny but that he granted to do thus much at the request of the brethren, being thereunto in a manner enforced: therefore it has more colour, and is more disputable, that he was too easily entreated and too ready to obey; and yet he does not admit that which some men say, that it went not well with Paul because, taking upon him a new and unwonted person, he did not so constantly as he was wont maintain the liberty purchased by Christ. He confesses indeed that God does oftentimes punish foolish purposes with unhappy success, Calvin says, but he sees not why this should be applied to Paul, who through voluntary subjection sought to win the favour of the rude and such as were not thoroughly instructed, that he might do them good, being about to do that not willingly but because he had rather yield to the brethren than stick to his own judgment. His courtesy rather deserves great praise, Calvin says, in that he not only gently abases himself for the unskilful people's sake but also defers to their foolishness who did unworthily and against reason suspect him: he might well have expostulated with them because they had been so ready to believe reports contrary to his reputation, and in that he abstains he shows great patience, while in that he wins their favour so carefully it is singular modesty. Moreover he might have been more severe on James and his fellows in office, Calvin adds, because they had not been more diligent to root out errors from among the people, for though it is certain that they taught faithfully, yet it may be that the sight of the temple, and the very seat of the law, did hinder them in defending the use of liberty; but Paul, whether he went from his right of his own accord or thought that they saw better what was expedient than he, acquiesces in their counsel. And whereas false Nicodemites, following this example of Paul, go about to colour their treacherous dissimulation whilst they pollute themselves with all filthiness of Popery, Calvin concludes, it needs no long refutation: they boast that they do this to win the weak brethren, as if Paul did yield to them in all things without choice; if, being Jews, they should take upon them according to the prescript of the law to fulfil among the Jews a vow infected with no idolatry, then might they prove themselves to be like Paul, but forasmuch as they wrap themselves in gross and altogether wicked superstitions, and that because they will escape the cross, what likeness is there in what they feign.

Albert Barnes says it is evident that James and the elders meant that these four men were connected with them in the Christian church, and that this shows the Christians at Jerusalem did not disregard the institutions of Moses and had not been so far enlightened in the doctrines of Christianity as yet to forsake the ceremonial rites of the Jews. From the mention of shaving the head it is evident that the vow they had taken was that of the Nazarite, Barnes says, and that as the time of their vow was about expiring they were about to be shaven, in accordance with the custom usual on such occasions; these persons Paul could join, and thus show decisively that he did not intend to undervalue or disparage the laws of Moses when those laws were understood as mere ceremonial observances. The purifying refers to the vows of sanctity which the Nazarites were to observe, Barnes says: they were to abstain from wine and strong drink, to eat no grapes moist or dried, to come near no dead body nor make themselves unclean for father, mother, brother or sister when they died, and to present an offering when the days of the vow were completed. To be at charges with them means to share with them the expense of the sacrifices and offerings required when the vow is completed, Barnes says, those offerings being a ram of a year old for a burnt-offering, a sheep of the same age for a sin-offering, a ram for a thank-offering, a basket of unleavened cakes and a libation of wine. It might be expedient for Paul to do what could not be enjoined on the Gentiles, Barnes says: they could not command the Gentile converts to observe those ceremonies, while yet it might be proper, for the sake of peace, that the converts to Christianity from among the Jews should regard them. The conduct of the Christians at Jerusalem in giving this advice, and of Paul in following it, may be easily vindicated, Barnes says: if it be objected, as it has been by infidels, that it looks like double-dealing, that it was designed to deceive the Jews in Jerusalem and to make them believe that Paul actually conformed to the ceremonial law when his conduct among the Gentiles showed that he did not, we may reply that the observance of that law was not necessary in order to justification; that it would have been improper to have enjoined its observance on the Gentile converts as necessary, and therefore it was never done; that when the Jews urged its observance as necessary to justification and salvation Paul strenuously opposed this view everywhere; and yet that as a matter of expediency it might be done. Paul took the men to himself and united with them in observing the ceremonies connected with their vow, Barnes says, and to transactions like this he refers when he says that unto the Jews he became as a Jew that he might gain the Jews: thus it has always been found necessary in propagating the gospel among the heathen not to offend them needlessly but to conform to their innocent customs in regard to dress, language, modes of travelling, sitting and eating, and Paul did nothing more than this, violating none of the dictates of honesty and truth. To signify means announcing to the priests in the temple his purpose of observing this vow with the four men, Barnes says, it being proper that such an announcement should be made beforehand. Charles Ellicott says the advice was eminently characteristic, since it came from one who himself lived as bound by the Nazarite vow, no razor having come upon his head and he drinking neither wine nor strong drink, as Hegesippus reports in Eusebius; by connecting himself with such a vow Paul would show that he was content in these matters to follow in the footsteps of James, and that he looked upon the observance of the Nazarite vow, if not as binding, at any rate as right and praiseworthy. It is obvious also that Paul's conduct on his last visit to Jerusalem had furnished a precedent for the line of action now recommended, Ellicott says, for he had then come as a Nazarite himself, had in that character burnt the hair which he had cut off at Cenchreae, and had offered the accustomed sacrifices, so that we may ask why he should not repeat the process now. There was, however, this difficulty, Ellicott says: the minimum period of the Nazarite vow was thirty days, and as Paul had not taken the vow previous to the advice, and probably wished to leave Jerusalem soon after the feast, it was out of his power to fulfil it now in its completeness. Jewish usage, however, made an intermediate course feasible, Ellicott says: a man might attach himself to a Nazarite, or company of Nazarites, join in the final process of purification which lasted probably for seven days, shaving his head and offering sacrifices with them, and this was considered in itself a devout act, especially if the newcomer defrayed the cost of the sacrifices, as Agrippa the First had in this way gained credit with the Jews as showing his reverence for the Law. It is clear that the four men were members of the Church of Jerusalem, Ellicott adds, and the fact is interesting as showing how intensely Jewish that church still was in its observances. To purify with them involved sharing their abstinence for the uncompleted term of the vow and shaving the head at its conclusion, Ellicott says, and to be at charges with them is literally to spend money on them, which involved payment for the act of shaving the head, for which probably there was a fixed fee to priest or Levite, and for the sacrifices which each Nazarite had to offer, namely two doves or pigeons, a lamb, an ewe lamb, a ram, a basket of unleavened bread, a meat offering and a drink offering. James adheres still to the terms of the concordat sanctioned at the council of Jerusalem, Ellicott says: he has no desire to withdraw any concession that was then made, and the Judaisers who in Galatia and elsewhere were in his name urging the necessity of circumcision were acting without authority; he thinks it fair to call on Paul to show that he too adheres to the compact and has no wish to disparage the customs of the Law, and Paul readily acts upon the suggestion. All promised well, Ellicott says, but an interruption came from an unexpected quarter and overturned what seemed so wisely planned in the interests of peace. The process lasted for seven days, probably reckoned from the completion of the thirty days or other term of the vow itself, Ellicott says, and Paul, having made himself the representative of the Nazarite company, had to give in their name the formal notice to the priests, who were to be ready for the sacrifices when the seven days had expired; seven days was the ordinary period for the more solemn purifications. A.T. Robertson says the elders had thought out a plan of procedure by which Paul could set the whole matter straight, and that the four were apparently members of the Jerusalem church with a temporary Nazarite vow whose completion was marked by several offerings in the temple and the shaving of the head. It was considered a work of piety to relieve needy Jews from the expenses connected with this vow, as Page says and as Paul does here, Robertson notes, and the two readings would mean either that they had taken the vow voluntarily or that the vow lies on them still. The imperative for purifying is a first aorist passive, Robertson says, and it is possible to see the full passive force here, be purified, but a number of aorist passives supplant the aorist middle forms and preserve the force of the middle, so that purify thyself is allowable; the word occurs in Numbers for taking the Nazarite vow, and the point is that Paul takes the vow with them. Spend money upon them is a first aorist active imperative of an old verb meaning to incur expense, Robertson says, and Ramsay argues that Paul had use of considerable money at this period, perhaps from his father's estate, since the charges for five men would be considerable, while Furneaux remarks that a poor man would not have been treated with the respect paid him at Caesarea, on the voyage and at Rome. The verb for walking orderly is an old one meaning to go in a row, to walk in a line or by rule, Robertson says: the rule is the law, and Paul was not a sidestepper. James himself presided at the Conference and offered the resolution that was unanimously adopted, Robertson says, and he stands by that agreement and repeats the main items from which the Gentiles are to keep themselves, having thus again cleared the air about the Gentiles who have believed; he asks that Paul will stand by the right of Jewish Christians to keep on observing the Mosaic law, and he has put the case squarely and fairly. Paul was conforming to the letter, Robertson says, joining the four men in their vow of separation and declaring to the priests what day he would report the fulfilment; and the question arises whether Paul acted wisely or unwisely in agreeing to the suggestion of James. What he did was in perfect harmony with his principle of accommodation when no principle was involved, Robertson says: it is charged that here he was unduly influenced by considerations of expediency and was willing for the Jewish Christians to believe him more of a Jew than was true in order to placate the situation, and Furneaux calls it a compromise and a failure, but he does not so see it, since to say that is to obscure the whole complex situation. What Paul did was not for the purpose of conciliating his opponents the Judaizers, who had diligently spread falsehoods about him, Robertson says, but solely to break the power of these false apostles over the thousands in Jerusalem who had been deluded by his accusers, and so far as the evidence goes that thing was accomplished, since in the trouble that comes at Jerusalem and Caesarea the Judaizers cut no figure at all. The explosion that came on the last day of Paul's appearance in the temple was wholly disconnected from his offerings for the four brethren and himself, Robertson says: it must be remembered that Paul had many kinds of enemies, and the attack on him by these Jews from Asia had no connexion whatever with the slanders of the Judaizers, which slander was put to rest forever by his following the advice of James, justifying the wisdom of that advice and Paul's conduct about it.

Adam Clarke says that from the shaving of the head mentioned immediately after, it is evident the four men were under the vow of Nazariteship and that the days of their vow were nearly at an end, since during the time of the Nazariteship the hair was permitted to grow and was only shaven off at the termination of the vow. Among the Jews it was common to make vows to God on extraordinary occasions, Clarke says, and that of the Nazarite appears to have been one of the most common, and it was permitted by their law for any person to perform this vow by proxy; it was also customary for the richer sort to bestow their charity on the poorer sort for this purpose, for Josephus observes that Agrippa, on being advanced from a prison to a throne by the Emperor Claudius, came to Jerusalem and there ordered very many Nazarites to be shaven, furnishing them with money for the expenses of that and of the sacrifices necessarily attending it, as Bishop Pearce reports. To be at charges with them is rather to be at charges for them, Clarke says, that is to help them to bear the expense of that vow, eight lambs and four rams besides oil and flour being the expenses on this occasion. The advice to show that he walked orderly and kept the law perhaps meant no more than that he should show by such means as were now in his power that he was not an enemy to Moses and that he still considered the law to be holy, Clarke says; Paul did so, and bore the expenses of those who from a scruple of conscience had made a vow and perhaps were not well able to bear the expense attending it. Had they done this in order to acquire justification through the law, Paul could not have assisted them in any measure with a clear conscience, Clarke says, but as he did assist them it is a proof that they had not taken this vow for that purpose, since vows rather referred to a sense of obligation and the gratitude due to God for mercies already received than to the procuring of future favours; and besides, God had not yet fully shown that the law was abolished, tolerating it till the iniquity of the Jews was filled up, and then by the destruction of Jerusalem sweeping every rite and ceremony away with the besom of destruction. To signify the accomplishment means declaring it, Clarke says, and as this declaration was made to the priest the sense is that Paul, taking the four men, began to consecrate himself with them, entering into the temple and publicly declaring to the priests that he would observe the separation of a Nazarite and continue it for seven days, at the end of which he would bring an offering according to what the law prescribed; but it is likely that Paul made no offering for himself and was merely at the expense of theirs. However we may consider this subject, Clarke says, it is exceedingly difficult to account for the conduct of James and the elders, and of Paul, on this occasion, and there seems to have been something in this transaction which we do not fully understand. He then reports the charge at length, that besides their typical and religious use sacrifices were also intended for the support of the state and civil government, the allotments to the priests being like civil-list money in other nations; that on these principles some have accounted for Paul's sacrificing after the commencement of the Christian dispensation, an action which has been severely censured by some as the greatest error of his life, since hereby he not only gave too much countenance to the Jews in their superstitious adherence to the law of Moses after it was abrogated by Christ, but his offering these typical sacrifices after the antitype of them was accomplished in the sacrifice of Christ was a virtual denial of Christ and of the virtue of his sacrifice; and that Paul's long trouble, which began immediately after this affair, some have looked upon as a judgment of God upon him for this great offence. But if this action were really so criminal as some suppose, Clarke answers, one cannot wonder enough that so good and so wise a man as Paul should be guilty of it, and that the Apostle James and the other Christian elders should all advise him to it; it is likewise strange that we find no censure ever passed on this action by any of the sacred writers, not even by Paul himself, who appears so ready on other occasions to acknowledge and humble himself for his errors and failings, but on the contrary reflects with comfort on his having complied with the customs of the Jews in order to remove their prejudices against him and his ministry and against the Gospel which he preached. John Wesley says they doubtless meant this advice well, but asks whether Paul could follow it in godly sincerity, and whether the yielding so far to the judgment of others was not too great a deference to be paid to any mere men. Ought he not, without any reverence to man, where the truth of God was so deeply concerned, to have answered plainly, I do not keep the Mosaic law, neither need any of you, Wesley asks: yea, Peter does not keep the law, and God himself expressly commanded him not to keep it, ordering him to go in to men uncircumcised and to eat with them, which the law utterly forbids. Then Paul took the men, yielding his own judgment to their advice, which seemed to flow not out of spiritual but carnal wisdom, Wesley says, seeming to be what he really was not, making as if he believed the law still in force; and declaring means giving notice to the priests in waiting that he designed to accomplish the days of purification till all the sacrifice should be offered, as the Mosaic law required.

debates: Whether Paul was right to take the vow: Wesley condemns it as a yielding to carnal wisdom and a seeming to be what he was not, and says Paul should have answered plainly that he did not keep the law and none of them need keep it; Clarke, of the same school, confesses the transaction is exceedingly difficult to account for, reports the charge that it was the greatest error of Paul's life and a judgment of God, and answers that no sacred writer ever censured it and Paul himself reflects on it with comfort; Barnes vindicates it in four steps against the objection of double-dealing; Calvin denies that Paul dissembled but grants that the charge of his being too easily entreated has some colour; Robertson answers Furneaux, who calls it a compromise and a failure, that the aim was to break the Judaizers' power over the deluded thousands and that this was accomplished; Ellicott calls it wisely planned in the interests of peace

What the four men and their vow show: Ellicott finds it interesting that they were members of the Jerusalem church, as showing how intensely Jewish that church still was; Calvin says that though they are reckoned among the faithful their vow was superstitious, and that the elders had fallen into a foolish indulgence through too much love of their nation; Barnes takes the same fact to show that the Jerusalem Christians had not yet been enlightened enough to forsake the ceremonial rites

Whether the concordat left Jewish believers free: Ellicott says James adheres to the terms agreed at the council and that the Judaisers urging circumcision in his name acted without authority; Robertson says James, who had presided and moved the resolution, asks Paul to stand by the right of Jewish Christians to go on observing the law; Calvin meets the objection that the elders free the Gentiles in plain words while leaving the Jews in bondage, answering that like liberty was granted to both but the Jews would not take what they might well have claimed

How Paul could join a vow he could not complete: Ellicott explains that the minimum term was thirty days, which Paul could not now serve, but that usage allowed a man to attach himself to a company of Nazarites for the final seven days of purification, especially if he paid for the sacrifices
outliers: Ellicott's citation of Hegesippus that James himself lived under the Nazarite rule, so that the advice came from a man bound by the same vow
The same passage of Josephus on Agrippa paying for many Nazarites to be shaven, cited independently by Ellicott and by Clarke through Bishop Pearce
Calvin's use of the episode against the false Nicodemites, who plead Paul's example to colour their dissimulation while wrapping themselves in wicked superstitions to escape the cross
Clarke's theory that sacrifices also served as the support of the state, the priestly allotments answering to civil-list money in other nations
Ramsay's argument, reported by Robertson, that Paul had command of considerable money at this period, perhaps from his father's estate
Calvin's remark that Paul might have been severer with James and his colleagues for not rooting out the errors, the sight of the temple perhaps hindering them in defending liberty

27.pericope_label: As the seven days drew to a close the Jews from Asia seize Paul in the temple, crying that he teaches against the people, the law and the place

schools.summary: John Gill says the Syriac version renders it that the seventh day was come, from the time that Paul came to Jerusalem, and that some understand this of the seven weeks from the passover to Pentecost, and that it was when they were almost ended and the day of Pentecost was at hand, for which Paul came up to Jerusalem; but rather the seven days of purification of the Nazarites are meant. On the cry for help Gill says the Arabic and Ethiopic versions read, help us, that is, to hold Paul, on whom they had laid their hands, and to assist in beating him; but why such an outcry for help against a single man, and he but little of stature and weak in body, and so easily held and overpowered, Gill asks, unless it may be they chose to engage others with them to give the greater countenance to their actions, and for their own security and protection, should they be opposed or called to an account. John Calvin says it is certain that these men were enemies to the name of Christ and of Christians, so that whilst Paul is bent to pacify the faithful he incurs the rage of the enemies: those of Asia are indeed the raisers of the tumult, but the minds of all the people were so corrupt with the hatred of him that they all became partners in the fury. But this place teaches that we must not take it impatiently if at any time our hope be frustrated, Calvin says, and our counsels, which we have taken with a right and holy affection, fall not out well, that our actions may have a happy end: we must attempt nothing but with a good conscience and according to the Spirit of God, but if things come not to pass as we would, even then let that inward feeling uphold us, that we know God approves our desire though it be laid open to the reproaches and mocks of men; neither let it repent us of our gentleness if at any time the wicked reward us otherwise than we deserve. They cry out as if they were in extreme danger, Calvin says, and they call upon all men to help them as if all religion were in hazard, whereby we see with what furious hatred they were inflamed against Paul, only because in showing that the full and perfect truth is found in Christ he taught that the figures of the law had an end. Now, whereas they conceive a false opinion, having seen Trophimus, they do more betray by this headlong lightness how venomous they be, Calvin says: they accuse Paul of sacrilege, because he brought into the temple a man which was uncircumcised, but they laid a most atrocious crime to the charge of an innocent through a false opinion. Thus the boldness of those men uses commonly to be preposterous who are carried away with an opinion conceived before, Calvin concludes; but let us learn by such examples to beware of the distemperature of affections, and not to let light prejudices have the rein, lest we run headlong upon the innocent, being carried with blind force.

Matthew Henry says we have here Paul brought into a captivity which we are not likely to see the end of, for after this he is either hurried from one bar to another or lies neglected, first in one prison and then in another, and can neither be tried nor bailed; when we see the beginning of a trouble, Henry says, we know not either how long it will last or how it will issue. He was seized in the temple, Henry says, when he was there attending the days of his purifying and the solemn services of those days: formerly he had been well known in the temple, but now he had been so long in his travels abroad that he had become a stranger there, so that it was not till the seven days were almost ended that he was taken notice of by those that had an evil eye towards him. In the temple, where he should have been protected as in a sanctuary, he was most violently set upon by those who did what they could to have his blood mingled with his sacrifices, Henry says, in the temple, where he should have been welcomed as one of the greatest ornaments of it that ever had been there since the Lord of the temple left it; the temple, which they themselves pretended such a mighty zeal for, yet did they themselves thus profane, and thus is the church polluted by none more than by popish persecutors, under the colour of the church's name and interest. The informers against him were the Jews of Asia, not those of Jerusalem, Henry says, the Jews of the dispersion, who knew him best and who were most exasperated against him.

Albert Barnes says the seven days were those which were to complete the observance of the vow, and that perhaps the whole observance in this case was intended to be but seven days, as the time of such a vow was voluntary. The translation, were almost ended, is not quite correct, Barnes says: the Greek implies no more than that the period of the seven days was about to be accomplished, without implying that it was near the close of them when he was seized, and by comparing a series of later passages in this book it appears, as Doddridge says, that the time of his seizure must have been near the beginning of those days. The Jews of Asia were those who resided in Asia Minor but who had come up to Jerusalem for purposes of worship, Barnes says. Men of Israel means all who are the friends of the law of Moses, Barnes says, and the words this is the man imply that they had before given information to the Jews at Jerusalem that there was such a man and now exulted in having found him, so that they called on all these to aid in securing and punishing him. They pretended that he taught that the customs and laws of the Jewish nation were not binding and endeavoured to prejudice all men against them, Barnes says; and everything against the law would be interpreted also as being against the temple, since most of the commandments of the law were celebrated there, while it is possible also that Paul might have declared that the temple was to be destroyed.
