The temple was surrounded by various areas called courts, Barnes explains, the outermost of which was called the court of the Gentiles and into that it was lawful for a Gentile to enter, but the word temple here refers doubtless to the parts of the area appropriated especially to the Israelites, which it was unlawful for a Gentile to enter; and he defiled the temple by thus introducing a Gentile, than which no greater defilement in their view could scarcely be conceived, so that no more effective appeal could be made to the passions of the people. Charles Ellicott says the phrase is literally that they were on the point to be completed, and that Luke speaks of the seven days as a definite or known period: they cannot refer, as some have thought, either to the duration of the vow, which was never less than thirty days, or to that of the Feast of Pentecost, which at this time was never extended beyond one, and must therefore be understood of the period of special purification which came at the final stage of the fulfilment of the vow. The Jews were from Asia, those who had come up to keep the Feast at Jerusalem, Ellicott says, and we may well believe they had been watching the Apostle eagerly as he passed in and out of the courts of the Temple; as it was, they seized him with all the tokens of his purification still upon him, about to offer sacrifices, and raised a cry which was sure to throw the whole city into an uproar. They first reiterate the general charge, Ellicott says, and in doing so bring against Paul, in almost identical terms, the very accusation which he had brought against Stephen, of which they thus make themselves the witnesses; and this was backed up by a more specific indictment, that he had brought Greeks, that is uncircumcised Gentiles, into the Holy Place, beyond the middle wall of partition which divided the court that was open to strangers from that which none but Jews might enter. The recent excavations of the Palestine Exploration Society have brought to light a slab with an inscription, discovered and deciphered by Clermont-Ganneau, which illustrates the horror with which the Jews looked on such a profanation, Ellicott says, its contents showing that it must have formed part of the low wall just mentioned: no man of alien race is to enter within the balustrade and fence that goes round the temple, and if any one is taken in the act, let him know that he has himself to blame for the penalty of death that follows. This, accordingly, was the punishment which the Jews of Asia were now seeking to bring on Paul and on his friends, Ellicott says. A.T. Robertson says the seven days were those for which Paul had taken the vow, though there may be an allusion to the pentecostal week for which Paul had desired to be present, and that Paul had spent seven days at Troas and at Tyre and had planned for seven here if not more. It was on the last of the seven days, when Paul was completing his offerings about the vows on all five, that the incident occurred that was to make him a prisoner for five years, Robertson says. In the very act of honouring the temple these Jews from Asia raise a hue and cry that he is dishonouring it, Robertson observes: Paul was not known by face now to many of the Jerusalem Jews, though once the leader of the persecution after the death of Stephen and the outstanding young Jew of the day, but the Jews in Ephesus knew him only too well, some of whom are here at the pentecostal feast. They had plotted against him in Ephesus to no purpose, Robertson says, but now a new opportunity had come, and it is possible that the cry was led by Alexander, put forward by the Jews in Ephesus, who may be the same as Alexander the coppersmith who did Paul so much harm. Paul was not in the inner sanctuary but only in the outer courts, Robertson notes; the verb for stirring up the multitude is an imperfect meaning to pour together, to confuse, used twice of the same sort of confusion created by Demetrius in Ephesus, which the Jews from Ephesus had learned from Demetrius the silversmith; and they attacked and seized Paul before the charge was made. The cry for help is a present imperative of a verb meaning to run at a cry, as if an outrage had been committed like murder or assault, Robertson says, and the phrase for all men everywhere is alliterative. The charges against Paul remind one of those against Stephen, in which Paul had participated according to his own confession, Robertson says, and, like the charges against Stephen and Jesus before him, truth and falsehood are mixed: Paul had said that being a Jew would not save a man, he had taught that the law of Moses was not binding on Gentiles, and he did hold, like Jesus and Stephen, that the temple was not the only place to worship God; but Paul gloried himself in being a Jew, considered the Mosaic law righteous for Jews, and was honouring the temple at this very moment. Worse than his teaching is his dreadful deed, Robertson says: he actually brought Greeks into the temple, which he had a right to do if they only went into the court of the Gentiles, but these Jews mean to imply that Paul had brought Greeks beyond this court into the court of Israel. An inscription was found by Clermont-Ganneau in Greek, built into the walls of a mosque on the Via Dolorosa, that was on the wall dividing the court of Israel from the court of the Gentiles, Robertson says, death being the penalty to any Gentile who crossed over. The perfect tense of the verb for defiling marks a defilement that lasts, Robertson notes; and all this is the substance of the call of these shrewd conspirators from Ephesus, Jews and not Jewish Christians nor even Judaizers, who hated him for his work there and who probably spoke evil of the Way before the multitude, so that Paul had to separate the disciples from the synagogue. These enemies of Paul had now raised the cry of fire and vanish from the scene completely, Robertson concludes, and this charge was absolutely false, made out of inferences of hate and suspicion.

Adam Clarke says the Jews of Asia pursued Paul with the most deliberate and persevering malice in every place, and that it appears it was through them that the false reports were sent to and circulated through Jerusalem. This is the man that teacheth is as much as if they had said, this is the man concerning whom we wrote to you, who in every place endeavours to prejudice the Gentiles against the Jews, against the Mosaic law, and against the temple and its services, Clarke says. That he brought Greeks also into the temple was a most deliberate and malicious untruth, Clarke says: Paul could accomplish no purpose by bringing any Greek or Gentile into the temple, and their having seen Trophimus, an Ephesian, with him in the city only was no ground on which to raise a slander that must so materially affect both their lives. Josephus informs us, Clarke continues, that on the wall which separated the court of the Gentiles from that of the Israelites was an inscription in Greek and Latin letters which stated that no stranger was permitted to come within the holy place on pain of death; and with such a prohibition as this before his eyes, was it likely that Paul would enter into the temple in company with an uncircumcised Greek, so that the calumny refutes itself. John Wesley says that when after giving notice to the priests they were entering upon the accomplishment of those days, it was toward the beginning of them that Paul was seized, and that the Jews who were from Asia were some of those who came from Asia to the feast. Against the people means the Jewish nation, and the law that of Moses, and this place the temple, Wesley says; and as to bringing Greeks into the temple, they might come into the outer court, but the accusers imagined Paul had brought them into the inner temple and had thereby polluted it.

debates: When in the seven days Paul was seized: Barnes denies that the Greek means almost ended and concludes with Doddridge, from a chain of later dates, that the arrest fell near the beginning of them, and Wesley says the same; Ellicott and Robertson place it at the end, Robertson on the last day, while the offerings for all five were being completed

What the seven days were: Ellicott rules out both the vow itself, never less than thirty days, and the feast, never extended beyond one, and takes them for the special purification at the final stage; Gill reports the Syriac reading of the seventh day and the opinion that the seven weeks from passover to Pentecost are meant; Robertson allows an allusion to the pentecostal week besides the vow

How the charge stands to the truth: Robertson weighs it item by item, granting that Paul had said being a Jew would not save a man, that the law did not bind Gentiles, and that the temple was not the only place of worship, while denying the inference, since Paul gloried in being a Jew and was honouring the temple at that moment; Clarke calls the specific charge a deliberate and malicious untruth that refutes itself; Calvin says a false opinion formed from the sight of Trophimus betrays how venomous the accusers were; Barnes allows that Paul may have declared the temple would be destroyed

Who raised the tumult and why: Henry notes the informers were Jews of the dispersion, who knew him best and were most exasperated; Robertson traces them to Ephesus, where they had plotted in vain, and suggests the cry was led by the Alexander they had put forward, the very method of confusion being learned from Demetrius
outliers: The temple inscription cited three ways: Clarke has it only from Josephus, while Ellicott and Robertson both point to the actual slab found and deciphered by Clermont-Ganneau and published in eighteen seventy-one, Ellicott giving its full text
Robertson's irony that in the very act of honouring the temple Paul was accused of dishonouring it
Robertson's note that the accusers, having raised the cry of fire, vanish from the scene completely and are never produced against him
Henry's remark that his enemies would have had his blood mingled with his sacrifices, and that the church is polluted most by persecutors acting under colour of her own name
Calvin's lesson that we must not take it impatiently when counsels formed with a right and holy affection do not fall out well
Gill's aside that Paul was little of stature and weak in body, so that the call for help against one man needs explaining

29.pericope_label: The mob drags Paul from the temple and beats him, until the chief captain runs down with soldiers, binds him with two chains and carries him into the castle

schools.summary: John Gill says that they had seen Trophimus with Paul before, not in the city of Ephesus but in that of Jerusalem. John Calvin says we see in this place the vanity of the common people, which count Paul a condemned man before ever they hear him: that the city is in a tumult in a matter relating to godliness is no marvel, but this is a point of perverse zeal and mad rashness, in that they set themselves against Paul before they know his matter, for in this corruption of nature frowardness is joined with foolishness, so that those will readily of their own accord make haste to maintain an evil cause who can hardly be moved with many exhortations to do well. This is a hard case, that the whole world should be armed against us of a sudden through the persuasion of a few, Calvin says, but seeing it pleases the Lord it should be so, let every one of us prepare himself by such examples to suffer all manner of assaults and to abide all brunts. Assuredly the force of Satan appears therein, Calvin continues, in that he drives the people headlong into such rage that, when they have shut the doors of the temple, being not content with mean punishment, they conspire to put Paul to death; we must thus think with ourselves that Satan does prick forward the enemies of godliness, lest their rage, how cruel and troublesome soever it be, trouble us. On the other side appears the wonderful goodness of God, Calvin says, when he raises up the chief captain of a sudden that he may deliver Paul from death: he himself thought upon no such thing, but came to appease the tumult which was raised among the people, yet the Lord shows a more evident token of his providence, because Paul's life was delivered from such present danger without man's counsel; thus does he suffer the faithful not only to labour but to be almost oppressed, that he may deliver them from death more wonderfully. Luke calls him the tribune of the band improperly, Calvin says, seeing every chief captain was set over a thousand, which also appears by the text, where he says that the chief captain took with him centurions. Those whose fury neither the majesty of God nor yet the reverence of the temple could once stay begin to relent when they see a profane man, Calvin observes, whereby it appears that they were set on fire rather with barbarous cruelty than zeal; and whereas the chief captain binds Paul with chains, he declares thereby sufficiently that he came not to ease him. The unbelievers would attribute this to fortune, Calvin says, but the Spirit has depainted out unto us the providence of God as in a picture, reigning amidst the confused uproars of men; and though it be very hard that this holy minister of God is so shamefully handled, yet the equity of the chief captain is to be commended if he be compared with the Jews, for he binds him with chains as if he were some evil-doer, yet vouchsafes to hear him when he is bound, whom they did beat unmercifully, neither does he determine to handle him hardly before he knew his cause; yea, this was the best way to mitigate their cruelty, because they hoped that Paul should be punished immediately. The madness of the raging people betrays itself on every side, Calvin says: they make horrible outcries, whereof one is contrary to another, and nevertheless they desire with one consent to have him put to death who was convicted of no offence, and in the meanwhile we need not doubt but that they were blinded with a colour of holy zeal; but the truth of the cause well known makes men truly zealous, as it makes them true martyrs of God, while rage betrays devilish madness. Whereas mention is made of the camp or fortress, Calvin says, we must know that the soldiers placed to guard the city had a place trenched and fortified on every side which they might defend as if it were a castle, and from which they might beat back all assaults if any sedition were raised, for it had not been safe for them to be quartered up and down in various places, seeing the people were treacherous and the city troublesome. We gather that the place was high, Calvin adds, because Luke says that when they came to the steps Paul was carried by the soldiers; and whether the soldiers lifted him up on high that they might bring him safe to the camp, or he was thus tossed with the violence of the crowd, this was no office of favour, but the greater the cruelty of those which followed him was, the more plainly did God declare that he was favourable to his servant in sparing his life, lest, if he should have been murdered in the tumult, his death should have wanted due fruit.

Albert Barnes says that as Trophimus was with Paul in Jerusalem it was inferred that he would attend him everywhere, and that this is a most striking illustration of the manner in which accusations are often brought against others: they had seen him with Paul in the city and inferred therefore that he had been with him in the temple, not even pretending that they had seen him there, but the inference was enough to inflame the angry and excitable passions of the multitude. So in the accusations which men now often make of others, Barnes says: they see one thing, they infer another, they could testify to one thing but conclude that another will also be true, and that other they charge on them as the truth; if men would state facts as they are, no small part of the slanderous accusations against others would cease, and an end would be made of most of the charges of falsehood and error and heresy and dishonesty and double-dealing and immorality. If a statement is made it should be of the thing as it was, Barnes says: if we attempt to state what a man has done it should not be what we suppose he has done, and if we attempt to state what he believes it should not be what we suppose he believes. The city was agitated and thrown into commotion, Barnes says, and they drew him out of the temple under the pretence that he had defiled it, the evident design being to put him to death, while the doors leading into the courts of the temple were shut. This was evidently done in a popular tumult, as had been done in the case of Stephen, Barnes says, for they could not pretend that they had a right to do it by law. The band of Roman soldiers was stationed in the tower Antonia on the north of the temple, Barnes says, a tower built by John Hyrcanus, high priest of the Jews, and by him called Baris, which was beautified and strengthened by Herod the Great and called Antonia in honour of his friend Mark Antony; Josephus describes this castle as consisting of four towers, one of which overlooked the temple and which he says was seventy cubits high. In this tower a guard of Roman soldiers was stationed to secure the temple and to maintain the peace, Barnes says, and the commander of this cohort is here called the chief captain, the word denoting properly one who commanded a thousand men, while the band was the tenth part of a legion and consisted sometimes of four hundred and twenty-five soldiers, at others of five hundred, and at others of six hundred, according to the size of the legion; the name of this captain was Claudius Lysias. To be bound with two chains was to show to the enraged multitude that he did not intend to rescue any one from justice but to keep the peace, Barnes says, Paul's being thus bound convincing them of his determination that justice should be done in the case; probably he was bound between two soldiers, his right arm to the left arm of the one and his left arm to the right arm of the other, or if his hands and feet were bound it is evident that it was so done that he was able still to walk, and this was in accordance with the prediction of Agabus. Charles Ellicott says the face of Trophimus was naturally familiar to those who had come from the same city, and that they had seen the two together in the streets, possibly near the entrance of the Temple, and, hatred adding wings to imagination, had taken for granted that Paul had brought his companion within the sacred enclosure. Better, perhaps, there was a rush of the people, Ellicott says: Luke brings into something like a mental juxtaposition the pictures of the tumult at Ephesus and that at Jerusalem, and the Jews of Asia, among whom we may perhaps think of Alexander the coppersmith, working then as afterwards much evil against the Apostle, may have taken part in both. The shutting of the doors was obviously the act of the Levite gate-keepers, Ellicott says: the Apostle was dragged out, the crowd followed him, and they seized the opportunity to guard the sacred precincts against further profanation. The officer was captain of a thousand men, the cohort being the sixth part of the legion, Ellicott says, and they were stationed in the tower known as Antonia, built by Herod the Great and named in honour of the Triumvir, which stood on the north-west side of the Temple area, on a rock, with a turret at each corner and two flights of stairs leading to the arcades on the northern and western sides. The Roman garrison was obviously stationed there to command the crowds of pilgrims and was likely to be on the alert at a time like the Pentecost Feast, Ellicott says, while the Procurator Felix was for the time at Caesarea; the next verse shows that their appearance was sufficient at once to strike some kind of awe into the turbulent mob, and once again the Apostle owed his safety from violence to the interposition of the civil power, the beating seeming to have been rough treatment with the fists rather than any regular punishment. Looking to the usual Roman practices in the treatment of prisoners, Ellicott says, we may think of each chain as fastened at one end to the Apostle's arm and at the other to those of the soldiers who kept guard over him, and so shackled he was taken before the Chiliarch Lysias for a preliminary inquiry. We note the parallelism with the like confused clamour at Ephesus, which is described in exactly the same terms, Ellicott says; and the Greek word for castle literally means encampment, coming by a transition which reminds us of the connection between the Latin words for a camp and a castle to be applied to a regular structure of stone or brick, such as the Tower Antonia. A.T. Robertson says Luke adds the reason for the wild charges made against Paul, and that the Jews from Asia knew Trophimus by sight as well as Paul, having one day seen both of them together in the city, which was a fact, and having just seized Paul in the temple, which was another fact. They supposed, Robertson says, using a perfectly harmless word, but they did, as so many people do, put their supposed inference on the same basis with the facts: they did not see Trophimus with Paul now in the temple, nor had they ever seen him there, but simply argued that if Paul was willing to be seen down street with a Greek Christian he would not hesitate to bring him into the court of Israel, so that both were entitled to death, especially Paul; this is the way of the mob-mind in all ages, and many an innocent man has been rushed to his death by the fury of a lynching party. The verb for the city being shaken is a common one for violent motion and emotion, Robertson says, and is used later by Tertullus of Paul as the stirrer up of riots; the cry spread like wildfire over the city and there was a pell-mell scramble to get to the place of the disturbance. They were saving the temple by dragging Paul outside, Robertson says, the imperfect vividly picturing the act as going on, and curiously enough both verbs used here occur together about the arrest of Paul and Silas in Philippi; the doors between the inner court and the court of the Gentiles were shut with a bang and at once, but this was only the beginning, the preparation for the real work of the mob, since they did not wish to defile the holy place with blood, and the doors were shut by the Levites. The word for tidings is an old one for the work of informers and then the exposure of secret crime, found here only in the New Testament, Robertson says: the Roman guard during festivals was kept stationed in the Tower of Antonia at the north-west corner of the temple, overlooking it and connected by stairs, and the commander's name was Claudius Lysias, each legion having six tribunes so that each tribune had a thousand men if the cohort had its full quota. The plural for centurions shows that Lysias took several hundred soldiers along, a centurion with each hundred, Robertson says, and he ran down from the tower of Antonia in a vivid scene; the mob stopped beating Paul before the job was over because of the sudden onset of the Roman soldiers, and some ten years before, in a riot at the passover, the Roman guard marched down and in the panic several hundred were trampled to death. He was bound with two chains as a violent and seditious person, probably leader of a band of assassins, Robertson says, and Lysias repeated his inquiries who he was and what he had done. The idiom for some shouting one thing and some another is the same as at Ephesus, Robertson notes, and the word for the castle comes from a verb meaning to assign soldiers a place or to encamp, so that it means an encampment and here the barracks of the Roman soldiers in the tower of Antonia.

Adam Clarke says they tumultuously seized on Paul and drew him out of the temple, out of the court of the Israelites where he was worshipping, and the doors of the court of the Gentiles were shut, probably to prevent Paul from getting any succour from his friends in the city; for their whole proceedings show that they purposed to murder him, bringing him out of the court of the Israelites, that court being peculiarly holy, that it might not be defiled by his blood, and shutting the court of the Gentiles that they might have the opportunity unmolested of killing him in that place, since the court of the Gentiles was reckoned to be less holy than that of the Israelites. The chief captain was the Roman tribune, who had a troop of soldiers under him which lodged in general in the castle of Antonia, built at the angle where the northern and western porticoes of the outer court of the temple were joined together, Clarke says: this castle was built by John Hyrcanus, high priest of the Jews, was at first called Baris and was the royal residence of the Asmoneans as long as they reigned in Jerusalem, and was beautified by Herod the Great and called Antonia in honour of his friend Mark Antony, the temple being commanded by it as it stood on higher ground. Josephus describes this castle as having four towers, from one of which the whole temple was overlooked, and says that one of the towers was joined to the porticoes of the temple and had a double pair of stairs from it, by which soldiers in the garrison used to come down with their arms to the porticoes on the festival days to keep the people quiet, for, as the temple was a guard to the city, so this castle was a guard to the temple, Clarke reports. It seems therefore very plain, says Bishop Pearce as Clarke quotes him, that the place where the Jews were about to kill Paul was the court of the Gentiles, the porticoes being there, and that the chief captain came down there to his rescue; the name of this tribune was Claudius Lysias, and he ran down the stairs to the porticoes. He took him with great violence, probably meaning an armed force, Clarke says, and to be bound with two chains was to be bound between two soldiers, his right hand chained to the left hand of the one and his left hand to the right of the other. John Wesley says the gates were shut both to prevent any further violation of the temple and to prevent Paul's taking sanctuary at the horns of the altar. It was a rule among the Jews that any uncircumcised person who came into the inner temple might be stoned without further process, Wesley says, and they seemed to think Paul, who brought such in thither, deserved no better treatment. A cohort or detachment of soldiers belonging to the Roman legion, which lodged in the adjacent castle of Antonia, were stationed on feast days near the temple to prevent disorders, Wesley says, and it is evident Lysias himself was not present when the tumult began, being probably the oldest Roman tribune then at Jerusalem and as such the commanding officer of the legion quartered at the castle. Then the tribune, having made his way through the multitude, came near and took him, Wesley says, and how many great ends of providence were answered by this imprisonment: it was not only a means of preserving his life, after he had suffered severely for worldly prudence, but gave him an opportunity of preaching the Gospel safely in spite of all tumult, yea, and that in those places to which otherwise he could have had no access. He commanded him to be bound with two chains, taking it for granted he was some notorious offender, Wesley concludes, and thus the prophecy of Agabus was fulfilled, though by the hands of a Roman.

debates: Why the temple doors were shut: Ellicott says the Levite gate-keepers seized the chance to guard the precincts against further profanation; Robertson agrees the Levites shut them but gives the crowd's motive, that they did not wish to defile the holy place with blood; Clarke reverses it, holding they were shut to keep Paul from succour and to allow an unmolested killing in the less holy outer court; Wesley adds that it was also to prevent his taking sanctuary at the horns of the altar

What the mob's inference shows: Barnes turns it into a rule about accusation generally, that men see one thing and infer another and charge the inference as truth, so that if facts were stated as they are most slander would cease; Robertson sets out the same fallacy and calls it the way of the mob-mind in all ages; Ellicott says only that hatred added wings to imagination

How the rescue should be read: Calvin makes it a demonstration of providence, since the tribune intended only to quiet a tumult and God delivered Paul without man's counsel, suffering the faithful to be almost oppressed that he may rescue them more wonderfully; Ellicott says the Apostle again owed his safety to the interposition of the civil power; Wesley counts the ends of providence served by the imprisonment, which preserved his life and opened places otherwise closed to his preaching

Why Paul was chained: Barnes says it was to show the crowd that justice would not be cheated; Robertson takes it as the treatment of a violent and seditious man, probably a supposed leader of assassins; Wesley says the tribune took it for granted he was some notorious offender, and that so the prophecy of Agabus was fulfilled by Roman hands
outliers: Calvin's observation that men whom neither the majesty of God nor the reverence of the temple could stay began to relent at the sight of a profane soldier, which shows they were fired by cruelty rather than zeal
Calvin's correction of Luke's title, that tribune of the band is said improperly, since such an officer was set over a thousand, as the mention of centurions in the same verse shows
Robertson's note that ten years earlier a Roman guard had marched down in a passover riot and several hundred were trampled to death in the panic
Bishop Pearce's inference, reported by Clarke, that the attempted killing must have been in the court of the Gentiles, since the porticoes were there
Calvin's image of the Spirit painting the providence of God as in a picture, reigning amid the confused uproars of men
Wesley's parenthesis that the imprisonment preserved Paul's life after he had suffered severely for worldly prudence

35.pericope_label: Borne up the stairs from the mob, Paul asks leave of the tribune, who takes him for an Egyptian rebel, and speaks from the steps in Hebrew

schools.summary: John Gill says the stairs or steps led up to the castle, which was built upon a very high place, and quotes Aristeas to the same effect; that the multitude followed after the captain and the soldiers who had taken Paul from them; and that just as he had got to the top of the stairs and was about to go in at the door, Paul made his request. On the Egyptian, Gill reports Josephus as speaking of one who came out of Egypt to Jerusalem and gave out that he was a prophet, deceiving the people, whom he persuaded to follow him to the Mount of Olives where they should see the walls of the city fall at his command, so that through the ruins they might enter in; but Felix the Roman governor fell upon them, killed four hundred, took two hundred prisoners, and the Egyptian fled. The account which Josephus elsewhere gives, and Eusebius from him, is another, Gill notes: that a certain Egyptian false prophet did much more mischief to the Jews, being a magician, and having got himself believed as a prophet, came into the country of Judea and gathered together about thirty thousand persons whom he had deceived, whom he brought out of the wilderness to the Mount of Olives, designing thence to take Jerusalem by force and seize the Roman garrison and take the government of the people; but Felix prevented his design, meeting him with the Roman soldiers assisted by all the people. Paul was not of that country, much less that man, Gill says, but a Jew both by birth and religion, born of Jewish parents and brought up in the Jewish religion, though his native place was Tarsus, a city in Cilicia where it is placed by Pliny, Ptolemy and Mela, and which some think the same with the Tarshish of the Old Testament; and the captain gave him licence, which he could not well deny after Paul had so freely declared who he was and addressed him in so courteous a manner. John Calvin says Paul offered himself to defend his cause, which all the servants of God must do, for we must do our endeavour to make our integrity known to all men, lest through our infamy the name of God be blasphemed. But when the chief captain demands whether Paul be not that Egyptian which was a murderer, and which a little before had induced a body of men to revolt, Calvin says, let us learn that how modestly and quietly soever the ministers of Christ behave themselves, and howsoever they be void of all fault, yet cannot they escape the reproaches and slanders of the world; which thing we must note for this cause, that we may accustom ourselves to contumely, and that in well-doing we may be prepared to be evil-spoken of. When he asks him concerning the Egyptian he means not Theudas the sorcerer, as some men falsely suppose, Calvin says, of whom Gamaliel made mention in the fifth chapter and of whom Josephus speaks in his twentieth book of Antiquities; for besides that we read there that Theudas carried away only four hundred men, while the chief captain reckons up in this place four thousand and says that they were all murderers, which is more, Theudas raised that faction during the reign of an earlier emperor.

Albert Barnes says the stairs were those which led from the temple to the tower of Antonia, and quotes Josephus that the tower was situated at the corner of two cloisters of the court of the temple, that on the west and that on the north, erected on a rock of fifty cubits in height and standing on a great precipice, and that on the corner where it joined the two cloisters it had passages down to them both, through which the guards went several ways among the cloisters with their arms on the Jewish festivals. It was on these stairs, as the soldiers were returning, that the tumult was so great, or the crowd so dense, that they were obliged to bear Paul along to rescue him from their violence, Barnes says. Away with him means to death, Barnes notes, comparing the cry at the trial of Jesus. May I speak unto thee means may I have the privilege of making my defence before thee, or of stating the cause of this tumult, Barnes says, and the question whether he could speak Greek implies that if he could he might be permitted to speak: the Greek language was then almost universally spoken, and it is not improbable that it was the native tongue of the chief captain, for it is evident that he was not a Roman by birth, since he says later that he had obtained the privilege of citizenship by paying a great sum. The language which the Jews spoke was the Syro-Chaldaic, Barnes says, and as the officer took Paul to be an Egyptian Jew he supposed from that circumstance also that he was not able to speak Greek. That Egyptian was probably a Jew who resided in Egypt, Barnes says, and Josephus has given an account of him which strikingly accords with the statement recorded by Luke: he came from Egypt to Jerusalem, said that he was a prophet, and advised the multitude of the common people to go with him to the Mount of Olives, saying that he would show them from thence how the walls of Jerusalem would fall down and promising to procure them an entrance through those walls when they were fallen. Josephus adds that he got together thirty thousand men that were deluded by him, whom he led round about from the wilderness to the mount called the Mount of Olives, being ready to break into Jerusalem by force from that place, Barnes says, but Felix, apprised of his movements, marched against him with the Roman soldiers, discomfited him, slew four hundred of them and took two hundred alive, while the Egyptian escaped out of the fight and did not appear any more. It was natural that the Roman tribune should suppose Paul to be this Egyptian and that his return had produced this commotion, Barnes says; and the mention of the wilderness corresponds remarkably with the account of Josephus, who says the Egyptian led them round about from the wilderness, the wilderness being the wild and uncultivated mountainous tract lying to the east of Jerusalem between it and the Jordan. It is another striking coincidence showing the truth of the narrative, Barnes adds, that neither Josephus nor Luke mentions the name of this Egyptian, though he was so prominent and acted so distinguished a part; but there is a remarkable discrepancy between the chief captain and Josephus, the latter saying that there were thirty thousand men. Paul was a Jew by birth, of Tarsus, a city not obscure or undistinguished, Barnes says, so that he could claim an honourable birth so far as the place of his nativity was concerned: Tarsus was much celebrated for its learning and was at one time the rival of Alexandria and Athens, Xenophon calling it a great and flourishing city and Josephus saying that it was the metropolis and most renowned city among the Cilicians. Beckoning with the hand was waving the hand as a sign that he was about to address them, and to produce silence and attention, Barnes says; and he used the Hebrew tongue, then a mixture of Chaldee and Syriac called Syro-Chaldaic, doubtless in preference to the Greek because it was better understood by the multitude and would tend to conciliate them if they heard him address them in their own language. The following chapter should have been connected with this, Barnes adds, since the division here is unnatural. Charles Ellicott says this was one of the flights of stairs leading from the tower to the Temple area, and that here the violence of the crowd became greater as they were more pressed in, so that the soldiers had literally to lift him from his legs and carry him in, while the troops lined the staircase on either side. We remember that the self-same cry away with him had been raised at the time of the Crucifixion, Ellicott says, and that it was used now with the same meaning with which it had been used then. The chiliarch apparently expected his prisoner to have spoken Hebrew, that is Aramaic, and was surprised to hear Greek, Ellicott observes, while the people expected Greek and were surprised at Hebrew; nothing could better illustrate the familiarity of the population of Jerusalem with both languages. The Greek has an illative particle which is wanting in the English, Ellicott says, so that it reads, art not thou then that Egyptian, this being the inference drawn by the chief captain from the fact that his prisoner spoke in Greek. The Egyptian was a false prophet who, a short time before this under the procuratorship of Felix, had led a great number of men to the Mount of Olives, promising them that they should see Jerusalem destroyed, Ellicott says: his followers were routed by Felix but he himself escaped, and the chief captain infers from the tumult raised by a Greek-speaking Jew that the Egyptian must have reappeared, this being probably one of the vague reports in the confused clamour of the multitude. The words of the question have, however, been taken on grammatical grounds in a different sense, Ellicott says, as though it meant, thou art not then that Egyptian, his speaking Greek having changed the chiliarch's previous impression; but against this there is the fact that an Egyptian Jew, coming from the very land of the Septuagint, would naturally speak Greek, and the inference that Paul was not the Egyptian because he knew that language would hardly be intelligible. Josephus gives a much larger number, Ellicott says, but his statistics in such cases are never to be relied on; and the word for murderer, literally dagger-bearer, was applied to the cut-throat bands who about this period infested well-nigh every part of Palestine, and who differed from the older robbers in being, like the Thugs in India, more systematically murderous, their presence in the siege of Jerusalem tending to aggravate all its horrors. The boast of being a citizen of no mean city was quite a legitimate one, Ellicott says, since in addition to all its fame for culture the town of Tarsus bore on its coins the words for an independent metropolis. Paul's position on the stairs raised him above the people, Ellicott says, and the characteristic gesture commanded instant attention; and he spoke, not as they expected in the Greek, which belonged to one who fraternised with Gentiles, but in the Hebrew or Aramaic which he had studied at the feet of Gamaliel. It was a strange scene for that Feast of Pentecost, Ellicott concludes: the face and form of the speaker may have been seen from time to time by some during his passing visits to Jerusalem, but there must have been many who had not heard him take any part in public action since the day when, twenty-five years before, he had kept the garments of those who were stoning Stephen; and now he was there, accused of the self-same crimes, making his defence before a crowd as wild and frenzied as that of which he had then been the leader. A.T. Robertson says the word for stairs is a late one found in the New Testament only here and at the close of the chapter, and that the verb for bearing means to take up with the hands, literally as here. Cheated of their purpose to lynch Paul, they were determined to have his blood, Robertson says, and the words away with him are the very ones used by the mob to Pilate when they chose Barabbas in preference to Jesus; he will hear it again from this same crowd, and Luke does not say that this mob demanded crucifixion for Paul, who was learning what it was to share the sufferings of Christ as the sullen roar of the mob's yells rolled on and on in his ears. The calm self-control of Paul in the presence of this mob is amazing, Robertson says, and his courteous request to Lysias was in Greek, to the chiliarch's amazement. The question expects the answer yes and the particle argues the matter, Robertson says, meaning the well-known Egyptian who had given the Romans so much trouble; the word for assassins is a Latin one for a man who carried a short sword under his cloak, and Josephus uses this very word for bands of robbers under this Egyptian. Josephus says that there were thirty thousand who gathered on the Mount of Olives to see the walls of Jerusalem fall down, and not merely four thousand as Lysias does here, Robertson notes, but Lysias may refer to the group that were armed thus, the core of the mob of thirty thousand; and Lysias at once saw by Paul's knowledge of Greek that he was not the famous Egyptian who led the Assassins and escaped himself when Felix attacked and slew most of them. In contrast with the wild guess of Lysias, Paul tells briefly who he is, Robertson says: a Jew by race, of Tarsus in Cilicia by country, and proud of it, one of the great cities of the empire with a great university. The phrase for no mean city is litotes again, Robertson notes, the same litotes used by Euripides of Athens, and there is an effective assonance, as Page calls it, in the words for city and citizen; it was a strange request and a daring one, to wish to speak to this mob howling for Paul's blood. Standing on the stairs makes a dramatic scene, Robertson says: Paul had faced many audiences and crowds but never one quite like this, and most men would have feared to speak, but not so Paul, who will speak about himself only as it gives him a chance to put Christ before this angry Jewish mob who look on him as a renegade Jew, a turncoat, a deserter, who went back on Gamaliel and all the traditions of his people, and who not only turned from Judaism to Christianity but went after Gentiles and treated them as if they were on a par with Jews. He shook down to the multitude with the hand, Robertson says, and waited till much silence had come, speaking in the Aramaean which the people in Jerusalem knew better than the Greek, for Paul could use either tongue at will. His enemies had said in Corinth that his bodily presence was weak and his speech contemptible, Robertson concludes, but surely even they would have to admit that Paul's stature and words reach heroic proportions on this occasion, self-possessed with majestic poise as he faces the outraged mob beneath the stairs.

John Chrysostom observes how, when Paul discourses to those that are without, he does not decline availing himself of the aids afforded by the laws: here he awes the tribune by the name of his city, as elsewhere he said that they had cast into prison, openly and uncondemned, men who were Romans. Since the tribune said, art thou that Egyptian, Chrysostom says, he immediately drew him off from that surmise; then, that he may not be thought to deny his nation, he says at once, I am a Jew, meaning his religion. What then, Chrysostom asks: did he deny that he was a Christian? God forbid, for he was both a Jew and a Christian, observing what things he ought, since indeed he, most of all men, did obey the law, as in fact he elsewhere calls himself under the law to Christ, which means the man that believes in Christ; and when discoursing with Peter he says, we, Jews by nature. This is a proof that he does not speak lies, seeing he takes all as his witnesses, Chrysostom says, and observe again how mildly he speaks; this again is a very strong argument that he is chargeable with no crime, his being so ready to make his defence and his wishing to come to discourse with the people of the Jews. Mark the providential ordering of the thing, Chrysostom says: unless the tribune had come, unless he had bound him, he would not have desired to speak for his defence, he would not have obtained the silence he did; and standing on the stairs there was the additional facility afforded by the locality, that he should have a high place to harangue them from, in chains too. What spectacle could be equal to this, Chrysostom asks, to see Paul, bound with two chains, and haranguing the people, and to see how he was not a whit perturbed, not a whit confused, but, seeing so great a multitude all hostility against him and the ruler standing by, first of all made them desist from their anger, and then how prudently he does it. Just what he does in his Epistle to the Hebrews he does here, Chrysostom says: first he attracts them by the sound of their common mother tongue, then by his mildness itself; and mark his address, at once so free from all flattery and so expressive of meekness, for he says not Masters, nor Lords, but Brethren, just the word they most liked, saying in effect, I am no alien from you, nor against you.

Adam Clarke says the stairs were those already mentioned, and that away with him means kill him, despatch him, for so much this phrase always means in the mouth of a Jewish mob. Claudius Lysias was not a Roman, Clarke says, having purchased his citizenship of Rome with a great sum of money, and it is very likely that he was but imperfectly acquainted with the Latin tongue; the tumult and the discordant noise prevented him from clearly apprehending what was said, and as he wished to know the merit of the cause he asked whether Paul understood Greek, and when he found that he did, proceeded to question him. The history to which Lysias refers is taken from Josephus, Clarke says: an Egyptian whose name is not known pretended to be a prophet and told his followers that the walls of Jerusalem would fall down before them if they would assist him in making an attack on the city, and he had address enough to raise a rabble of thirty thousand men and advanced with these as far as the Mount of Olives; but Felix, the Roman governor, came suddenly upon him with a large body of Roman troops, both infantry and cavalry, the mob was speedily dispersed, four hundred killed, two hundred taken prisoners, and the Egyptian himself with some of his most faithful friends escaped, of whom no account was ever afterwards heard. As Lysias found such an outcry made against Paul he supposed that he must be some egregious malefactor, and probably that Egyptian who had escaped, Clarke says; learned men agree that Luke refers to the same fact of which Josephus speaks, but there is a considerable difference between the numbers in Josephus and those in Luke, the former having thirty thousand and the latter only four thousand. The small number of killed and prisoners, only six hundred in all according to Josephus, leads us to suspect that his number is greatly exaggerated, Clarke argues, since six hundred in killed and prisoners out of a mob of thirty thousand routed by regular infantry and cavalry is no kind of proportion, but it is a sufficient proportion to a mob of four thousand. Dean Aldridge has supposed that the number in Josephus was originally four thousand, Clarke reports, but that ancient copyists mistaking the Greek letter for four wrote thirty thousand instead; and there is another way of reconciling the two historians, which is that when this Egyptian impostor at first began to make great boasts and large promises a multitude of people, to the amount at least of thirty thousand, weary of the Roman yoke, readily arranged themselves under his banners, but as he performed nothing that he promised, six and twenty thousand of these had melted away before he reached Mount Olivet, and this remnant the Romans attacked and dispersed. In the notes on an earlier chapter it is shown that Tarsus was a city of considerable importance and in some measure a rival to Rome and Athens, Clarke says, and that because of the services tendered to the Romans by the inhabitants Julius Caesar endowed them with all the rights and privileges of Roman citizens; when Paul calls it no mean city he speaks a language that was common to those who have had occasion to speak of Tarsus, Xenophon calling it a great and flourishing city, Josephus the metropolis and most renowned city among the Cilicians, and Ammianus Marcellinus a very respectable city that adorns Cilicia. Paul stood on the stairs where he was out of the reach of the mob and surrounded by the Roman soldiers, Clarke says, and beckoned with the hand, waving it, which was the sign that he was about to address the people, as Virgil says of Turnus that he beckoned with his hand and cried out with a loud voice, bidding the Rutulians desist and the Latins cease from throwing their javelins. He spake to them in what was called the Hebrew tongue, that is the Chaldaeo-Syriac, Clarke says, very well expressed by the Codex Bezae as in their own dialect; and never was there a more unnatural division than that in this chapter, since it ends with a single comma, the best division having been at the end of the twenty-fifth verse. John Wesley notes the stairs by which Paul was borne up, the mob following, and the tribune's question about the Egyptian, and observes that Paul spoke in the Hebrew tongue, that is in the dialect then commonly used at Jerusalem.

debates: What the tribune's question means: Ellicott says the Greek particle makes it, art not thou then that Egyptian, the guess being drawn from Paul's Greek, and he argues against the alternative rendering, thou art not then that Egyptian, since an Egyptian Jew from the land of the Septuagint would naturally speak Greek; Robertson takes precisely that alternative, holding Lysias saw at once by Paul's Greek that he was not the Egyptian

How the numbers are to be reconciled with Josephus: Ellicott dismisses the difficulty, since his statistics in such cases are never to be relied on; Robertson supposes Lysias means only the armed core of the larger mob; Clarke offers a harmony, that six and twenty thousand had melted away before Olivet, and reports Dean Aldridge's conjecture that copyists mistook the Greek letter for four and wrote thirty thousand, supporting it by the disproportion of six hundred casualties to thirty thousand men

Why Paul chose Aramaic: Barnes says it was better understood by the multitude and would conciliate them; Ellicott adds that they expected Greek from one who fraternised with Gentiles and got instead the tongue he had learned at the feet of Gamaliel; Chrysostom says he first attracted them by the sound of their common mother tongue and then by his mildness, addressing them not as Masters or Lords but as Brethren

What the arrest accomplished: Chrysostom marks the providence, that unless the tribune had come and bound him Paul would neither have wished to speak nor have obtained silence, and that the high place gave him a pulpit; Robertson calls the same moment heroic, recalling that his enemies at Corinth had said his bodily presence was weak and his speech contemptible
outliers: Ellicott's close, that many in the crowd had not seen Paul act in public since the day, twenty-five years before, when he kept the garments of those who stoned Stephen, and that he now faced the same charges before a mob as frenzied as the one he had led
Chrysostom's question what spectacle could equal the sight of Paul bound with two chains and haranguing the people
Dean Aldridge's palaeographic conjecture, reported by Clarke, that a copyist mistook the Greek numeral for four and turned four thousand into thirty
Ellicott's comparison of the dagger-bearers to the Thugs of India, as more systematically murderous than the older robbers
Clarke's parallel from Virgil, where Turnus beckons with the hand and bids the Rutulians desist
The complaint of both Clarke and Barnes that the chapter division is unnatural, Clarke noting that it ends at a single comma
